**Another SQL bug avoided by verifying rather than trusting.** `receipt_given` is INTEGER, and the generic migration loop adds every column as TEXT, which would have returned the string "1" on a device that already had `harvest_dispositions` from 1.0.34.22 while a fresh install returned the number 1. Given its own typed `ALTER TABLE`, the second time that exact trap has come up today. Every new column and the new money-given query were then run against a scratch database.

**Three shell-escaping casualties in one build, worth recording because the cost keeps repeating.** Writing test code through a quoted heredoc mangled a regex into `$?` (invalid), truncated a string literal at `', and a trade needs no money anywhere.** Direct extension of the income work: "A sale via a harvest could be through a trade as well, and not monetary. They could have traded their extra potatoes for ears of corn, etc. In that case the receipt of goods would go directly into the kitchen as part of the food inventory."

 or backticks: **write the patch script with the file tool, not through the shell.** `node --check` on a generated script before running it would have caught all three immediately.

`scripts/test_harvest_trade.js` is 95 checks, up from 64. Three mutations confirmed to break the new ones. `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every touched file, bare-text audit 0, schema guard clean, all eleven suites passing. No reference-database change. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Most recent (2026-09-05, 1.0.34.22): surplus harvest sold, traded or given away, and a trade needs no money anywhere.** Direct extension of the income work: "A sale via a harvest could be through a trade as well, and not monetary. They could have traded their extra potatoes for ears of corn, etc. In that case the receipt of goods would go directly into the kitchen as part of the food inventory."

**Three things can happen to a surplus and they are structurally different**, which is why this is its own record rather than an income row with a price invented for it: sold puts money in, **traded puts GOODS in**, given puts nothing in. The middle one is real economic activity with no money in it at any point, and it is the one every budgeting tool either ignores or fakes a price for.

**One disposition is three moves, and they happen together.** The harvest comes down through the same `consumeKitchenItem` cooking already uses, so a harvest drawn down by trading and one drawn down by eating go through one path rather than two that can drift. For a trade, each thing received becomes a kitchen row with a new `'trade'` source, so the inventory can say how a jar of honey got there and never counts it as bought. For a sale, an income entry is written and can carry an income stream, so surplus reaches the income figures rather than sitting in its own corner.

**WHAT A TRADE IS WORTH, WHICH IS MOSTLY NOTHING.** This app already settled the general question the austere way: where the garden covered a grocery line, that is a **count of lines that did not have to be bought, never a dollar saving**, because what the produce would have cost is unknown. A trade gets one narrow exception, and it turns on a real distinction: if there is a **recorded price** for the food received, from an actual past grocery trip, then "what would this have cost me" is not unknown, it is measured from that person's own shopping. So it can say "8 kg of corn at the $2.40 a kg you paid on 2026-08-14, about $19.20 you did not spend."

**Two hard rules on that figure, both tested.** It is an **avoided cost and never income** ("money you kept, not money you earned"), because no money arrived and letting it reach the income mix would put money that does not exist into the "$X a month across N streams" total. And it is only computed when the recorded price's unit **matches** what was received: a per-package price has no per-kilo meaning without a size, and converting would be the invented number again by a longer route. Same refusal `mergeShoppingAmounts` already makes about crossing weight and volume.

**What was given is never valued**, at either end. Nobody knows what their own potatoes were worth, and valuing both sides would also double count one event. A test confirms the potato's own recorded price is never used even when one exists.

**A real bug caught by testing SQL against a scratch database rather than trusting `tsc`.** `getLastPaidPrices` aliased a column `AS on`, and **ON is a reserved word**: SQLite raises a syntax error only when the statement is prepared, so `tsc` was clean and it would have thrown at runtime. Renamed to `paidOn`, with the reason written into the function so nobody renames it back. Every new statement was then run against a scratch database, including the receipts cascade.

**Quantities are never added across units** in the surplus summary: 3 kg of beans and 3 bunches of beans are two lines, not 6 of anything. Keyed by food AND unit, and a mutation collapsing that key fails.

**Deleting a disposition deliberately does not reverse it.** Deleting the note of an event does not un-happen it: the corn is in the kitchen and the potatoes are gone. Putting either back would edit an inventory to match a record, which is the wrong way round.

`scripts/test_harvest_trade.js` is 64 checks. Four mutations confirmed to break it, including converting across mismatched units and adding quantities across units. `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every touched file, bare-text audit 0, schema guard clean, all eleven suites passing. No reference-database change. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Most recent (2026-09-05, 1.0.34.21): income streams that vary, which is all the interesting ones.** Direct question: "Do we have a way to track multiple income streams? For instance, what if the user had a goal to add solar panels to their home so they can be able to feed more electricity into the grid than they use and could then receive a small monthly income from it? Or, maybe they sell their extra harvests, or do some other work on the side."

**The answer split, and checking it was the useful part.** Several income streams were already possible: `finance_recurring` holds any number of income rows, so a paycheck beside a pension was fine. But it stores ONE amount and treats it as what arrives every month, and **all three examples given are income that does not do that.** Solar feed-in varies with sun, season and what the house used. Harvest sales vary with what is ripe and stop entirely for months. Side work varies with whether there was work. So the app could represent the boring stream and not one of the three asked about. Separately, `summarizeRecurring` collapsed every source into one `monthlyIncome`, so nothing reported income per stream at all.

**A variable stream has no amount to type. It has a history.** So the amount becomes a declared guess and the real figure is measured from receipts tagged to the stream, which is the same call already made for market-rate accounts earlier the same day: measure what happened rather than apply an assumed rate. `checkEstimate` then compares the two and says how far off the guess was, refusing under 3 months because one payout is not a trend.

**THE DECISION THAT CARRIES THE MOST RISK, and it is one line.** The average divides by the whole span from first receipt to last, **not** by the months that had money in them. Harvest sales earning nothing from October to April are earning nothing in those months. Dividing only by the summer would turn "about $60 a month across the year" into "about $120 a month" by quietly dropping the winter, and the flattering version is the one a naive implementation produces. Tested from both sides with the same three summer sales, once alone and once inside a six-month span, confirming the average roughly halves and that the wording explains why empty months are counted.

**The solar question is answerable honestly because both halves are measured.** A stream can point at the goal that created it (`from_goal_id`), so `payback` takes the goal's money cost against receipts that actually arrived. It refuses under 3 months, because a rate from two payouts is arithmetic rather than information, and **flags anything under 12 months, because a seasonal stream has not yet been through its own quiet season** and a figure from three summer months is flattering. The rate is always stated as the rate so far, never as what it will do. Remaining months round UP, so the estimate is never optimistic, and a test asserts `monthsAtThisRate * averagePerMonth >= stillToRecoup`.

**Two new income categories**, both things this app is in an unusual position to track since it already knows about a garden: energy sold back to the grid, and produce or goods sold. Filing them under Investment or Something else would have made a trend in either invisible.

**The mix, and one thing worth knowing for its own sake.** `buildIncomeMix` reports each stream's share, and flags when one is 70% or more of the total, because several streams are only diversification if none of them is nearly all of it. A single stream alone is deliberately NOT flagged: saying one income is 100% of one income tells nobody anything, and a mutation removing that guard fails.

**A schema bug caught before it shipped.** `amount_is_estimate` is INTEGER in the CREATE TABLE, and the generic migration loop adds every column as TEXT. Left in that loop, a device that already had the table would have returned the string `"1"` while a fresh install returned the number `1`, so every `=== 1` check would have passed on one and failed on the other. Split into its own conditional `ALTER TABLE` with the right type, and the read compares through `Number()` as a belt-and-braces guard.

**A fixture of mine was wrong again, and the test said so.** The twelve solar amounts sum to 920, not the 1020 I asserted, so four checks failed on my arithmetic rather than on the code. Corrected, with the figures derived in the test rather than hand-typed.

`scripts/test_finance_income.js` is 88 checks. Five mutations confirmed to break it, including the two that matter most: averaging over earning months only, and rounding payback down. `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every touched file, bare-text audit 0, schema guard clean, all ten suites passing. No reference-database change. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Named and now closed the same day (1.0.34.22):** selling harvest was two unconnected acts, a `garden_harvests` draw-down and an income receipt, with nothing linking them. Closed along with trading and giving away, which turned out to be the more interesting half.

**Most recent (2026-09-05, 1.0.34.20): spending tagged to a goal, closing the double-entry gap named an hour earlier.** Direct instruction: "Do the entry tagging so a purchase counts toward a goal."

**It tags a COST LINE, not a goal**, and that is the load-bearing decision. A goal can carry several money costs (Lumber, Hardware, Delivery), and the line is the only level at which an amount means anything, since contributions are per-line in that line's own unit. Tagging the goal alone would leave the app unable to say which cost a purchase advanced.

**Money costs only, and that is not a simplification.** A dollar entry cannot advance a line counted in hours or jars, so `listGoalCostOptions` filters to `kind = 'money'` on ACTIVE goals. Active only as well: tagging spending to a goal already reached or set aside would quietly move a figure someone has finished looking at.

**Expenses only, enforced at the write rather than trusted from the form.** `createEntry` drops the tag on an income row, and switching the form to income clears it, so a stale tag cannot be saved and then silently ignored. The reasoning: money going OUT advances a cost; income tagged to a goal would be earmarking, which is a different idea and one this app cannot act on because it does not move money. **Setting money aside needs no special case**, since the Set Aside category group is already an expense here, so "put $200 by for it" tags correctly through the same path.

**Read where it lives, never copied.** `listGoalsWithProgress` sums tagged expenses in SQL and adds them to hand-recorded contributions, so correcting a price in Spending corrects the goal too. Copying into a contribution row would have left a stale figure on the goal the moment a price was fixed, which is the exact drift this project keeps having to unpick.

**The one risk this opens, and how it is handled.** Both routes can put money in, so the same $200 can be recorded twice. The app genuinely cannot tell one $200 from another on the same day, so it does not try: `GoalCostProgress` now carries `fromSpending` and `recordedByHand`, and when both are non-zero the line says so and names the risk. Same honesty rule the grocery list already turns on, where money read from where it lives is reported as already counted with a note not to enter it again.

**The split is DERIVED from the total rather than passed in beside it** (`recordedByHand = contributed - fromSpending`, with `fromSpending` clamped into range), so the two halves cannot add up to something other than the whole. Three mutations confirm it: letting the halves exceed the total, suppressing the both-sources flag, and trusting an out-of-range breakdown all fail the suite.

**Tagged spending had to move everything hand entry moves**, or a cost could read as met while still being asked for monthly. Tested: it can meet a line on its own, it fills the bar, it makes `pace` refuse as already-met, and it reduces the cross-goal monthly figure to only what is still short.

`scripts/test_finance_goals.js` is 111 checks, up from 86. `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every touched file, bare-text audit 0, schema guard clean, all nine suites passing. `goal_cost_id` added with the established conditional `ALTER TABLE` pattern, so no reference-database change and no re-import. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Most recent (2026-09-05, 1.0.34.19): Goals, pass 3 of the Finances rebuild, and the one idea that keeps it from being a savings tracker.** Asked for with its own framing, given twice: "goals require costs to attain each goal, whether that cost is a trade of time, or goods, or actual money."

**That framing is the design rather than a detail, and it is why costs are their own table.** Every budgeting app has a savings goal: a number, a date, a bar. This app already tracks harvests with real remaining quantities, ferments, therapy sessions with real `duration_minutes` and exercise with real minutes, so it can model a goal whose cost was never money without inventing anything. Rebuilding a raised bed costs lumber AND a weekend; a year of preserves costs jars, produce and hours. One amount column could only ever have held the money.

**THE CENTRAL RULE: COSTS OF DIFFERENT KINDS ARE NEVER BLENDED.** A goal needing $500 and 20 hours, with $250 and 10 hours in, is not "50% done". It is half funded and half worked, which are two facts. And $500 with zero hours is not 50% either: the money is finished and the work has not started. Turning hours into dollars at an assumed rate would make one confident number out of two honest ones, which is the invented figure this app refuses everywhere. **There is deliberately no single percentage for a goal anywhere in the feature**, and a test asserts the `GoalProgress` object exposes no `fraction`, `percent` or `progress` field and that the wording contains no `%` at all.

**What is reported instead is how many costs are met plus which is furthest behind**, and that second figure is the useful one: it answers whether the thing holding someone up is money or a weekend, which a single percentage cannot say.

**"Furthest behind" is ranked by SHARE, not amount, and that is not cosmetic.** 40 hours short and $40 short are not orderable; 90% short and 10% short are. **The test for this was initially worthless and caught by mutation testing**: both fixtures happened to rank the same way under either rule, so inverting the comparison in the source changed nothing. Rebuilt around a case where the two rules genuinely disagree (9 of 10 short against 200 of 1000 short, so the smaller amount is the proportionally worse line), plus its mirror so the answer is not just list position. This is the same bad-fixture trap already hit once the same day in the payoff suite, which is twice now: **a fixture where two candidate rules agree tests neither.**

**One unit per cost line, which removes conversion from the feature entirely.** A line carries its own unit and every contribution to it is in that unit by construction, so there is no hours-to-minutes or grams-to-pounds arithmetic anywhere and nowhere for it to be wrong. Money never carries a unit at all, enforced at the write so the display cannot print a dollar amount followed by "hours".

**Money is the only kind summed across goals**, precisely because it is the only kind measured in one unit. Outstanding time and goods costs are **counted**, never totalled, and the summary says plainly that they are not added into one number. A dated money cost contributes its per-month figure; one without a date is counted separately so the total is not read as complete.

**The refusals, each tested:** no target date gives no per-month figure and names the missing piece rather than returning zero; a date this month puts the whole remainder in this month rather than dividing by zero months; a passed date reports overdue and never a negative monthly amount; a cost line with a target of zero is **not** met, since calling it met would mark a whole goal done; a goal with no costs is not silently complete and is described as a note rather than something trackable.

**Reached and set aside are both kept rather than deleted.** A goal that was met is worth looking back at, and one abandoned is a decision rather than a mistake to erase. Both stop asking for anything each month, and a set-aside goal keeps every contribution for when it gets picked back up.

**Measured rather than eyeballed, on both surfaces the icon actually sits on.** `#AF88F2` is **2.53:1** against `menuSurface` (both hub menus and Home's new lens menu) and **2.83:1** against a composited card surface. Both are under the 3:1 floor this project holds non-text marks to. `#C7ACF6` clears both, at 3.53:1 and 3.96:1.

**Five call sites, not one.** The report was about Home's new lens menu, but the same glyph in the same wrong shade was in TabHub's grid, Home's Digest flip cards, the Digest category header, and the Digest's own LensHub override. Fixed by making `PurpleRibbonIcon`'s `color` prop **optional with `tabPurpleDigestText` as its default** and dropping the explicit colour at all five sites, so there is one answer rather than five that can drift. The prop stays for a caller that genuinely needs another shade, since a ribbon on a filled button would want `textOnPrimary` and neither of these.

**Worth noting for the next reader:** `TabHub`'s ribbon was passing `route.color`, which comes from `TAB_ROUTES` and is by definition the fill colour. Any icon taking its colour from that list inherits the same question, and this one was the only case where the fill token was being asked to carry a shape rather than sit behind text.

`tsc` clean, `eslint` at the pre-existing baseline (one unescaped apostrophe in `index.tsx`, confirmed present at 3a0fb9e), bare-text audit 0, schema guard clean, suites unaffected and re-run. **Not yet confirmed on-device**, and this one is a visual judgment: whether the lighter ribbon now reads clearly on the grey menu rather than merely measuring better.

**Most recent (2026-09-05, 1.0.34.13 through 1.0.34.17): the kitchen inventory, built out from a read-through into a real loop.** Five versions, one architecture, described directly: "Anything they make or grow should become part of the Kitchen inventory the moment they are harvested or completed... Making the meals requires stock on hand, or items to be purchased based on usage and needs... There will be non-food items needing to be tracked as well, which should be a different inventory from their food item inventory, but both available to be on the grocery list, clearly labeled as non-food item."

**Kitchen, on the Life tab** (`components/KitchenSection.tsx`, `lib/kitchenDb.ts`, the `kitchen_items` table). On Life rather than Food because what is in the house is a household-running concern like bills are, and every Food lens is a BUILDER, something you make. Three sources feed one view: garden and fermentation harvests keep their own tables (a harvest has a lifecycle a pantry item does not), and `kitchen_items` holds what someone added and what a ticked grocery line put there. Ticking a line adds it, and the price panel behind it corrects the size, so a 750 ml bottle is recorded as 750 ml rather than the 250 ml a recipe wanted. **A row already drawn down is left alone**: someone has started using it, and rewriting the amount underneath them would discard what they recorded.

**The foundation, and a correction worth keeping.** I first claimed grocery lines carried "name only". They carry `category` + `food_name`, and for a schedule-derived line `food_name` IS `base_name` (see `resolvePurchasableNames`), the same canonical key `food_purchase_forms` is keyed on, so those already matched, by a coincidence nobody had written down. What was genuinely missing is the link to the food ITSELF: nutrients, scores, condition relevance, all dropped at the grouping step where `entry.foodId` was in hand. Identity now flows recipe to shopping list to grocery line to kitchen item, TEXT rather than INTEGER to match what actually flows (the builders' own column type, sometimes a composite like `1234|Scanned`). Matching files each row under **every key it can be found by** and looks up in order: reference row, canonical pair, bare name.

**A household inventory beside the food one**, 63 everyday consumables in 7 groups (`constants/householdItems.ts`). Separate because almost everything this app does with a food is meaningless for bleach, so one list would have half its rows silently opting out of every feature around them. **Nothing is typed but the amount**: household picks from that catalogue, food picks from `food_purchase_forms`, the 212 canonical purchasable foods. **No staples list was written for food**, deliberately, since that table already IS the canonical set and a second one would drift. Durable goods and medicines are both absent on purpose, the second because prescriptions and supplements are already tracked in Schedule with interaction rules behind them.

**Making something moves stock both ways** (`lib/kitchenUsage.ts`, the action on `app/food-item-detail.tsx`, which covers all eleven builders in one screen). **It is never silent**: the plan is shown, then confirmed. Applying it off the back of a save would have been the fastest way to make the feature untrustworthy, because saving a recipe is not cooking it and the app cannot know whether someone used their own stock or something they picked up on the way home. A shortfall is reported, never invented. **The bug worth naming**, invisible until it has eaten an inventory: two ingredients resolving to the SAME stock row would each be told they could have all of it, so `buildMakePlan` keeps a running claim per row. Held by test, and the test verified by removing the tally.

**And the loop closes.** Any saved dish says on load whether it can be made, names the shortfall, and puts it on the grocery list carrying the food's identity, so what gets bought matches back next time. Absent rather than reassuring when the plan cannot be computed: a wrong "you have everything" sends someone to an empty cupboard.

`scripts/test_grocery_list_math.js` grew from 130 checks to 162. Failure output verified three separate times this session, each by reintroducing the exact bug: the column transposition, the purchase-counted-as-stock rule, and the shared stock row. `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every new and touched file, bare-text audit at 0 throughout. **The pieces are individually verified and the loop has never run end to end**, which is the check that matters: seed stock, open a dish you are partly short for, add the shortfall, tick it off, return and confirm it now reads as covered, then make it.

**Most recent (2026-09-05, 1.0.34.7 through 1.0.34.12): the TabHub and LensHub menus, reordered, recoloured and made to follow the ground theme.** One continuous piece of work across six versions, from a direct review of the tab colours.

**The order was never chosen.** Every tab after the original seven had been appended last, each for the sound reason that appending changes no existing tab's swipe adjacency, and ten tabs later that had produced a sequence nobody picked. `TAB_ROUTES` now reads in groups of three after Home: **Food/Schedules/Signals** is what you do daily, **Insights/Trends/Reports** is what it tells you, **Garden/Digest/Life** is the wider world. One correctness fix falls out of it: Signals is where symptoms are logged and Trends is the patterns drawn FROM them, so having Trends first put an output ahead of its own input. That list drives the menu, the swipe order and the header dots at once, so all three moved together. Dots include Home again (reversing 2026-08-21) but still exclude Profile and Info, which is a different call rather than the same one: those are Stack screens that cannot be swiped to at all.

**Home has its own corner menu**, replacing a Digest shortcut that made the corner mean "pick what you want to see here" on nine tabs and "go to The Digest" on one. It is **not a scroll-to**: every section on Home is a view onto a function living in another tab, so picking one goes to that function, exactly as tapping the card does. The one exception is From The Digest, whose card IS the content rather than a shortcut, so it scrolls to itself; marked by a `scrollTo` flag rather than special-casing a key. Ordered the same way TabHub is and **deliberately independent of Profile's Home ordering**, which applies to the page alone. Each icon wears the colour of the tab it leads to (new optional `LensOption.iconColor`), so grouping and colouring compound and the grid reads as blocks.

**The tab's name is gone from the top left of every lens popup**, since the corner button, the page identity box and the screen header all already say it. `CARD_HEADER_HEIGHT` deliberately stays in the card's height sum: the grid was laid out inside what remained, so reclaiming those 20px would lift every option on every tab.

**The active ring and the menu border both follow the ground theme now.** Taking `buttonColor` raw would have been a regression dressed as a feature: on `menuSurface` it measures 2.26:1 to 3.20:1, under the 3:1 floor on four of five themes and worse than the fixed teal it replaced at 3.60:1. Lightened by 0.35 it clears everywhere. Named in the code: the border used to match the header and footer lines, which still draw from the generic palette, so those no longer share a setting with it.

**The colour work, and the lesson from it.** Mint was wrong for Insights twice over: it read as fresh and growing, which is Food's and Garden's meaning, and measured 0.051 from `tabFood`, the closest pair in the palette, sitting directly beside it. **Blue turned out to be unreachable** because every blue light enough to clear the contrast floors lands on Trends or Schedules. Insights and Life exchanged colours instead. A rose from the one open hue arc was tried over the orchid and reverted within the hour: it measured better (0.130 against 0.094) and read as too bright on a real screen. **The numbers narrow the field; they do not pick.** Worst touching pair in the grid went from 0.051 to 0.067, and Garden/Digest swapped so the two greens stopped touching.

**Two things found by measuring rather than looking.** `IridescentRingCircle` had not been iridescent for some time and was renamed `ActiveRingCircle`. And `profileActive` in TabHub is permanently false: TabHub mounts inside the tabs group and Profile is a Stack screen outside it, so that menu is never open over Profile. Both are now commented rather than left for the next reader.

`tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every touched file, suites 30/142/29, bare-text audit at 0 throughout. **On-device confirmed:** "It looks good."

**Most recent (2026-09-05, 1.0.34.6): the two halves of Finances connected, after a one-line question that found a real hole.** Asked directly: "When they pay out, it needs to come from an account somewhere. Does it?"

**It did not.** Bills, income and recorded spending were a flow with no source; accounts were a stock nothing ever touched. Paying rent left checking exactly as it was, getting paid left it exactly as it was, and buying groceries on a card left that card's balance where it stood, which quietly made the payoff plan wrong. The two tables predate accounts (`finance_recurring` from 1.0.34.1, `finance_accounts` from 1.0.34.4) and nothing had ever joined them.

**The obvious fix is to decrement the balance, and it is the wrong one.** A balance here is typed by hand, and the app only ever sees the transactions someone bothered to record: not the coffee, not the bank fee, not a direct debit nobody set up as a recurring bill. Subtracting what it knows from a real balance produces a number that is confidently wrong within a month, and worse, one nobody can tell apart from a real one afterwards. This is the same call already made twice today for interest, and it holds harder here.

**So the balance stays exactly what was entered, on the date it was entered, and what the records say has happened since is reported beside it.** The gap between the two is not an error to resolve. It is the most useful thing on the screen: it says how much spending is going unrecorded.

**Three nullable columns** (`paid_from_account_id` on recurring and entries, `paid_to_account_id` on recurring), added with the established conditional `ALTER TABLE` pattern, so no reference-database change and no re-import. **Nullable and staying that way:** requiring an account would make the form worse for someone who only wants a monthly total, and would turn a bill someone knows about into one they cannot record until they have set up an account.

**The cutoff is where a wrong number was easiest to produce, and it is tested from both sides.** An entry dated BEFORE the balance was last confirmed is already inside that balance, and counting it again would report money as unaccounted for when it was accounted for. A liability also moves the other way: spending on a card increases what is owed while the same figures reduce an asset, and getting that backwards would show a card being paid down while it was being run up.

**A duplication this exposed, worth more than the feature that found it.** A car payment recorded as a bill AND as the loan account's minimum payment is one payment described in two places: the monthly total counted it, and the payoff plan counted it again. `duplicatedDebtPayments` reports it and **changes nothing**, since which of the two to keep is not the app's call and silently ignoring one would make a figure someone can see disagree with a figure they cannot. This is the same fault the due-date model was restarted over in 1.0.34.2, arriving from a different direction.

**Grocery lines and therapy sessions are deliberately not linked**, and the screen says so by omission rather than guessing: they are read where they live and carry no account of their own, so they count toward spending and not toward any one account's reconciliation. Adding an account column to `grocery_list_items` would be a reach into another feature for a figure that is already honest without it.

`tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every touched file, bare-text audit 0, suites 72/108/69/142/55/142/29/30. Four mutations confirmed to break the new gates. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Most recent (2026-09-05, 1.0.34.5): interest, and the discovery that the rate line was drawn in the wrong place.** Direct question: "Should things like Own: Investments, and Own: Retirement also be capable of tracking interest or compounded interest... Same would be for interest on a car loan or credit card."

**The answer splits three ways rather than two, and `carriesDebtTerms` was conflating two different things.** It meant "is a liability", so Savings could not hold an APY despite that rate being printed on a statement, while Investments would have been offered a field it has no honest value for. The real distinction is not asset against liability:

- **`stated`**: a rate written in a contract. Card APR, loan rate, savings APY. Interest is arithmetic.
- **`market`**: no rate exists. Investments, retirement, property. "7% average" describes decades of the past, not a rate anything is growing at, and applying it forward would put an invented number beside real balances.
- **`none`**: checking, cash.

Savings is the case that proves it: an asset with a stated rate. `rateKind` replaces `carriesDebtTerms`, and `carriesMinimumPayment` is derived separately from `side`, since an APY does not come with one.

**A gap in what shipped an hour earlier.** `apr` was stored but read ONLY inside the payoff simulation. A $4,200 card at 24.99% costs about $87 a month to sit there, and that appeared nowhere in Finances. `carryCost` and `totalMonthlyInterest` put it on the net-worth card, framed as what it is: **a bill in every sense except that nobody sends it to you.** Simple monthly interest (rate over 12) rather than a compounded effective rate, deliberately, because that is how a statement computes a finance charge and a figure arguing with the paper in someone's hand would be worse than none.

**For market accounts, measurement rather than projection**, which was the user's own call when asked ("Measured only, for now"). New `finance_account_balance_history`, per account, because **the aggregate net-worth table cannot answer how one account did and has a flaw that shows the moment you try: adding a NEW account jumps the total, and that jump is not growth.** `measuredChange` reports the annualized change between the first and last balance recorded, refusing in three cases that would each produce a confident wrong number: fewer than two points, under 30 days (a week's move scaled by 52 is arithmetic but not information), and a starting balance of zero, which has no ratio to grow by.

**The subtlety that decides whether the figure may be called a return at all: money paid in looks exactly like growth.** A balance rising from 40,000 to 46,000 could be a 30% return or a 5,000 deposit and 1,000 of growth. So updating a balance takes an optional "paid in or taken out", and the wording changes on it: with contributions recorded it is a return, without them it says plainly it is the change in the balance and that anything paid in is inside it. Both are tested with identical balances and a sixfold difference in the reported rate.

**A bug the tests caught in the wording.** A losing account reported its rate through `Math.abs`, so a 3,000 loss read as "about 8.3% a year" with nothing saying it fell. The direction now attaches to the rate itself ("a fall of about 8.3% a year"), not only to the amount. Two of my own rounding expectations were wrong in the same run and the code was right.

**One thing ruled out regardless: nothing auto-accrues a stored balance.** What was typed on a date is a fact with a date, and growing it silently would turn a record into a guess with no way to tell which was which. Computed figures sit beside the balance, marked, which is also the nudge to go update it.

`tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every touched file, bare-text audit 0, suites 72/108/69/123/55/142/29/30. Four mutations confirmed to break the new gates. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Named and not built:** forward projection ("where will this be in 20 years"), deliberately deferred rather than dropped. Doing it honestly needs the rate to be an input the person picks and the output labelled a scenario that never mixes into net worth, and it belongs with Goals, since a projection is how someone knows whether a goal is reachable.

**Most recent (2026-09-05, 1.0.34.4): the budgeting core, pass 2 of the Finances rebuild.** The ordinary ground pass 1 deliberately skipped, since the health-money layer was the half nothing else could replace. This half is the reason someone would not simply use Monarch instead.

**Accounts and net worth.** `lib/financeAccounts.ts` (pure, no database) plus `lib/financeAccountsDb.ts` and three tables. Balances are typed in, because the standing no-bank-connection rule is the point rather than a gap. **A net-worth point is recorded when a balance changes, not on a timer**, so the line only moves when something real did; a nightly snapshot would draw a flat line through months of nothing happening and make it look like data.

**Debt payoff, and the one finding worth keeping.** Snowball and avalanche are simulated month by month with a **rolling commitment**: the pool is the extra plus the sum of every minimum, fixed at the start and not recomputed from still-open debts. That was a bug caught by test, and it is the whole mechanism: a cleared debt's minimum has to keep flowing into the next one or the plan silently slows down. Expected 15 months, got 20.

**Then the test caught a false claim before it shipped.** The first wording said both orders finish in the same month, reasoning that the same amount goes out either way. **That is wrong, and the check named it: 37 months against 40.** Paying less interest leaves less to pay, so the cheaper order is usually also the shorter one. The wording now reports both figures, and states what smallest-balance-first is actually for as **a month** (its first debt gone in month 4 rather than month 22) rather than as a feeling, so it can be weighed against the interest instead of being the vague reassuring option. **Neither order is picked**, because which one someone will keep going with is not something an app can know.

**Budget limits per category**, in Spending. What repeating bills already commit is shown **beside** what has been spent rather than added into it: adding them would double-count the month a bill is both committed and paid, and they answer different questions. A limit the bills alone already exceed says so plainly, since that one cannot be met by spending less.

**Sinking funds**, in Coming Up, for anything arriving less often than monthly. Those are the bills most likely to wreck a month precisely because they sit outside its rhythm. The app does not move money and says so.

**`scripts/check_schema_sql.js` is new**, and it exists because the same mistake happened three times in three days: a backtick inside a SQL comment, which terminates the template literal every `CREATE TABLE` in this project lives inside. `tsc` always caught it, so it never shipped, but it points at a line of English prose rather than at the cause, which is what made it cost minutes each time. Verified both ways.

`tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every touched file, bare-text audit at 0, suites 72/108/69/80/55/142/29/30. Every new check confirmed able to fail by breaking it. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Named and not built: Goals**, asked for directly with its own framing: "goals require costs to attain each goal, whether that cost is a trade of time, or goods, or actual money." That last part is the design constraint rather than a detail, and it is why this is pass 3 rather than a field bolted onto sinking funds.

**Most recent (2026-09-05, 1.0.34.3): the health-money layer, pass 1 of a Finances rebuild, after a fair challenge that the first build was thin.** Asked directly: "What app did you look at to decide what should be in the finance lens? This is extremely minimal." **The honest answer was none.** Finances had been built from general knowledge of household bill categories without looking at a single real finance app, and it showed.

**What the gap turned out to be, once actually researched.** Every mainstream app (YNAB, Monarch, Copilot, Simplifi, Rocket Money) is built on things this had none of: accounts and balances, net worth, **a spending limit per category with progress against it**, debt payoff with snowball against avalanche, goals and sinking funds, a cash-flow forecast, a subscription audit, and month-over-month trends. The budget one is the worst of them: what shipped records what was spent and **never compares it to a plan**, which is the entire premise of YNAB and EveryDollar.

**But the bigger miss was building a generic household budget inside a chronic-illness app.** The money questions someone with a tracked condition actually has are where they stand against a deductible and out-of-pocket maximum, whether an FSA is about to be forfeited, whether a bill matches its Explanation of Benefits, and what a condition costs in a year. Pass 1 is that layer, because it is the only part that could not be replaced by a link to Monarch.

**Three things it does, and the reasoning that shaped each.** Deductible and out-of-pocket standing, with the plan year starting when the person's actually starts rather than in January, and a **starting offset** so beginning tracking in June does not report that nothing has been met. HSA and FSA kept apart on the one difference that costs money: FSA funds are forfeited and get a warning, HSA funds roll over and deliberately never do. And an EOB check whose whole value is what it leaves out: **the provider's billed amount is not in the equation.** Allowed minus what insurance paid is what is owed; billed above allowed is written off under the plan's contract, and treating that gap as owed is the most common way people overpay. A test breaks `checkBill` to use `billed` and confirms it then calls a perfectly normal EOB an error.

**Cost-per-condition reaches across four tables and infers nothing.** Medical bills, repeating health costs, one-off health spending and therapy sessions each gained a `condition_code`, and the rollup assembles whatever carries one. The app cannot know a $240 clinic visit was for Hashimoto's rather than a broken wrist, so it asks, and **untagged cost is reported on its own and never divided across conditions**, which would turn one honest figure into several invented ones. Repeating costs are scaled by months elapsed rather than shown at face value, using the rule-derived monthly factor so there is no second copy of that arithmetic.

`scripts/test_finance_health.js` is 69 checks. Failure output verified by making the EOB check use billed instead of allowed, which reports four failures including "billed far above allowed is not an error" and exits non-zero. `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean, bare-text audit 0, suites 30/142/29/55/108/72/69. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Named and queued, not built:** the budgeting core (accounts, net worth, per-category budget limits, debt payoff with snowball against avalanche, sinking funds) is pass 2, agreed as "both, health layer first". **Goals shipped as pass 3 on 2026-09-05 (1.0.34.19), and carried a reframing worth keeping**, given directly: "goals require costs to attain each goal, whether that cost is a trade of time, or goods, or actual money." That makes a goal something this app can model rather than a savings target, since it already tracks harvests, ferments and session time as things with real cost.

**Most recent (2026-09-05, 1.0.34.2): the due-date model rebuilt, an hour after Finances shipped.** Reported directly: "Sometimes a bill could be due on a specific day of the month, or the first, second, third, or fourth specific day of the week, per week, per every 2 or 3 weeks per month." Every one of those is a real bill and the shipped model could express only the first.

**Taking the report seriously surfaced a bug in what had just shipped.** `finance_recurring` stored a `cadence` word plus a `due_day` number, and an annual bill with a day of the month does not say WHICH month, so `upcomingBills` showed a yearly bill as due **every month**. Found by reasoning about the report rather than by a test, and it is now covered from both sides (`test_finance_schedule.js` and `test_finance_math.js`).

**The first attempt at a fix was scrapped and restarted**, on the user's own instruction and for a reason worth keeping: it kept `cadence` AND added a parallel due rule. That is the same fact stored twice, in a matrix where most combinations are meaningless (a weekly bill has no day of the month, a quarterly one needs a month a monthly one does not). **The rebuild stores one `DueRule` and derives how often from it**, so a contradiction cannot be represented at all.

**New `lib/financeSchedule.ts`** holds the whole model: four rule shapes (`everyNWeeks` 1-4 with a weekday and an anchor date, `dayOfMonth` every 1/3/6/12 months, `twiceMonthly`, `nthWeekday` with 1st through 4th plus Last), the date arithmetic, the wording, and a defensive parser. **Stored as JSON in one column** rather than six or seven nullable ones: nothing queries a bill BY its due rule in SQL, so the relational shape buys nothing and costs correctness, and the app already stores structured values this way (`payload_json`, `depth_data_json`).

**`scripts/test_finance_schedule.js` is 108 checks**, weighted at the four places date math actually goes wrong: month length (the 31st in February), nth-weekday offset (September 2026 starts on a Tuesday, so Tuesdays are 1/8/15/22/29 while Mondays are 7/14/21/28, and that asymmetry shifts everything), phase (every 2 weeks is meaningless without knowing which week, and must stay on the same weekday forever), and cycle anchoring (the bug above). Failure output verified by removing the month-length clamp, which produces the impossible **2026-02-31** the clamp exists to prevent and exits non-zero.

**Another trap found while writing it, now covered:** every 4 weeks is **13 payments a year, not 12**. A bill someone thinks of as monthly but actually pays every four weeks costs a whole extra payment a year, every year.

**Migration is honest rather than complete.** Only the unambiguous case is converted (monthly + a day of the month). Everything else never carried enough to place on a calendar, so it is left null rather than guessed at; those bills keep counting toward monthly totals through a clearly-marked legacy fallback, and `upcomingBills` now returns them as `needsSetup` so the screen **names them instead of dropping them**, which is what the shipped version did silently.

The form asks only what the chosen frequency needs, and previews the rule in words plus its next date before saving, built from the real rule so the preview cannot drift from what gets stored. `tsc` clean, `eslint` clean, bare-text audit 0, suites 30/142/29/55/108/72. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Most recent (2026-09-05, 1.0.34.1): Finances, the Life tab's first area.** Direct request: "Let's start with Finances, but think through everything, making sure to follow rules that other lenses already follow. Finances is much larger than just tracking a few numbers. Match life against finances in a logical way, setup for the average person and the average things they would have for bills and charges."

**"Match life against finances" is the whole design, and it turned out to mean reading rather than asking.** This app has been recording real, dated, priced grocery trips since 2026-09-01 (`grocery_list_items.price`) and real hands-on therapy costs since 2026-09-04 (`therapy_sessions.cost`). A finance area that made someone retype all of that would be worse than useless. So `getTrackedSpending` reads both **where they already live and copies nothing**. Copying into `finance_entries` was the obvious shortcut and the wrong one: correcting a price on the grocery list would then leave a stale finance copy disagreeing with it, which is precisely the drift this project keeps having to unpick. Grocery lines are totalled with `groceryLineTotal`, the grocery list's own already-tested function, rather than a second copy of arithmetic that has to know when a per-pound price needs a weight before it means anything.

**Two tables, because a plan and a record are different things.** `finance_recurring` is what is supposed to happen every month; `finance_entries` plus the tracked reads are what did. Collapsing them is how a budget stops being able to answer the only question worth asking, which is whether they match. Income and expenses share one table rather than getting one each: they are structurally identical (a name, an amount, how often, which day) and `direction` is the only difference, so splitting would mean two of every query.

**The arithmetic is the part that earns the test suite, and it is not obvious.** A month is not four weeks. Weekly is 52/12 = **4.33** times a month, and treating it as 4 understates a year by four whole payments, roughly 8%, compounding across every weekly line. Every two weeks (26 payments a year) and twice a month (24) look interchangeable and differ by two whole paychecks. `scripts/test_finance_math.js` is **93 checks**, and its failure output was verified by setting weekly to 4 and biweekly to 2, which reports "expected ~433.33, got 400" across seven checks and exits non-zero. **The suite also caught my own arithmetic slip** while being written: a test asserted rent due on the 1st would appear in a 14-day window from the 5th, when it is 26 days out. The code was right and the expectation was wrong.

**Due dates clamp to month length**, which is why `nextDueDate` is a function rather than a template string: a bill due on the 31st has to land on the 30th in April and the 28th in February, and unclamped it produces 2026-02-31, which downstream either rejects or silently rolls into March. Cadences that drift (weekly, every two weeks, twice a month) return null rather than a guessed date, and the Coming Up section says how many bills that leaves out rather than quietly dropping them.

**Two honesty rules carried over from the grocery list.** A grocery line with no price or a therapy session with no cost is **counted, never estimated**, and any total built over them says how many are missing and calls itself a floor. And where the garden or a ferment covered a grocery line, that is reported as **a count of lines that did not have to be bought, never a dollar saving**: those lines carry `sourced_from_kitchen` and deliberately carry no price, so what the produce would have cost is genuinely unknown, and pricing it would be the invented number this app refuses everywhere else.

**Structurally, Finances is one lens with four internal sections rather than four lenses**, and that is a decision about what comes next: Life is going to hold "a ton of things", so its lens list has to read as a list of AREAS. Four lenses named Overview / Bills / Spending / Coming Up would make Life look like a money tab and leave nowhere obvious for the second area. This follows Digest's lens-then-topic pattern, rendered with the pill row the app already uses for sub-navigation.

**Categories are an ordinary household's, not an accountant's**: 33 expense categories across Home, Utilities, Health, Food, Getting Around, Money Owed, Everyday, Set Aside and Other, plus 7 income kinds. Health and Food are deliberately finer-grained, since those are the two the app already knows real things about. **Set Aside is its own group** so savings is subtracted from what is left without being reported as an expense, because saving more should not read as costs rising.

**No bank connection, stated as a stance rather than a gap**, in the code and in the help text: this app holds health data on one device with no backend, and handing over a bank credential would give that up on the least defensible possible grounds.

**The backtick trap bit again**, second day running: a SQL comment used `` `direction` `` inside the schema template literal and terminated the string. Caught by `tsc` immediately both times. The rule is now simply no backticks in that block at all, and the whole CREATE TABLE region was swept to confirm none remain.

`tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every new and touched file, bare-text audit 0, suites 30/142/29/55/93. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Named and not done:** `treatments` has no cost column, so a monthly supplement and prescription spend has to be entered as an ordinary recurring bill rather than being read from My Meds the way groceries and therapies are. That is the obvious next link and it needs a column plus a My Meds field, not a change here.

**Most recent (2026-09-04, 1.0.33.4): Life, the tenth tab.** Direct request: "A new tab needs to be added and available through TabHub menu. The name of the new tab is Life. There will be a ton of things that will be included in Life... This will deal with the user's life, all aspects." Asked first, before building: which icon, and which are still free.

**The icon is `infinite`, chosen against the set rather than in isolation.** Seven of the nine existing tabs are concrete objects (a house, a plate, a stethoscope, a calendar, a chart, a compass, a document), and Life is not another domain beside them, it is the container the rest sit inside; an abstract mark among concrete ones says that before the label is read. Four candidates were ruled out for specific reasons rather than taste: **the butterfly is already a selectable TabHub BUTTON icon**, so it would have appeared twice on one screen; `diamond` reads as "premium" in an app with a real paid-tier model; `person` is Profile; `planet`/`earth` is the Digest's own Earth Matters. The solid twin of any outline a lens already uses was excluded too.

**The color is `#DE9CE2`, hue 296, and getting there produced a mistake worth recording.** The first suggestion was hue 255, reached by reading `tabProfile`'s own comment, which describes the palette as it stood the day that color was placed, including "Reports (280, purple)" for a hue that has since moved to the Digest and been rotated again to 262. Nothing in that comment is false; it is history written in the present tense. Read as the current layout it produced a value **7 degrees from the Digest**, which would have read as the same purple in the menu. Caught only because the request came back as "I don't know what hue 255 is" and answering that meant measuring every hex rather than re-reading the prose. **The narrow lesson, now written into `tabLife`'s own comment: when placing a color against its neighbors, compute the neighbors from the hex values, never from the comments describing them.**

Measured, the hues in use are 25, 45, 95, 140, 150, 195, 229, 262 and 330, plus Reports at zero saturation. That leaves exactly one wide gap, 262 to 330 at 68 degrees, whose midpoint is 296. Every other gap is 45 to 55 degrees between two tabs that already read as similar at small size, so filling one would have produced a fourth green, a second teal, or a red (which means danger everywhere else in this app). 296 keeps 34 degrees of clearance both ways, the same separation Schedules already holds from the Digest, and measures ~3.30:1 against `menuSurface`, clearing the standing 3:1 floor. A published [swatch page](https://claude.ai/code/artifact/ea5999d5-8320-4d7b-aaa9-7f479a7f247a) puts the nine on a hue wheel and shows 296 in a reproduction of the real TabHub grid, since a color chosen from a large swatch is a different color at 19 pixels on a grey pill.

**What shipped is the shell, deliberately and stated as such on the screen itself.** "A ton of things" was named without naming which things, so a guessed lens set would have meant building something to tear out. The tab is complete as a tab (in `TAB_ROUTES`, in the grid, swipeable, its own color, its own help, its own identity label) and its single Overview lens is an honest account of an empty room: what the tab is for, that nothing is in it, and that no placeholder features or dead buttons are present. Same treatment this app already gives Pattern Finder with no flares logged. Reports' precedent is followed for the single-lens case: keep the real LensHub anyway so the corner button behaves consistently.

**Two things fell out for free.** Every consumer of `TAB_ROUTES` derives dynamically (verified across all of `app/`, `components/`, `hooks/`), so TabHub, swipe adjacency, `GatedTabContent`, `LensHub` and Profile's per-tab background picker all picked Life up with no change. And **the grid now comes out even**: eleven items was an awkward 3/3/3/2, twelve is four full rows. `variant="field"` reuses the shared resting scene, the same choice Garden and Digest make, rather than generating a background for a tab with no content.

**One tooling note worth keeping:** `tsc` failed on `'/life'` not being a valid `Href`, because Expo Router's typed routes live in a generated, gitignored `.expo/types/router.d.ts` that only `expo start` refreshes, not `expo export`. Fixed by briefly running the dev server to regenerate, **not** by casting the path in `constants/tabs.ts`, which would have permanently silenced a real check in tracked code to work around a stale local cache.

`tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every touched file, bare-text audit 0. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Most recent (2026-09-04, 1.0.33.3): Profile's card order rebuilt around what each card affects.** Reported as a judgment rather than a bug: "I think the order of things in preferences needs to be reevaluated." Correct, and the diagnosis is that **the order was build history, not priority**. Garden Details sat second, above every health and food setting, because it was built early. **Conditions & Check-In sat fourth**, below Garden and Meal Timing, despite being the setting that reaches furthest into the rest of the app: condition scoring, Digest pinning, "Meals You Can Eat", recipe cautions, Insights personalization, Pattern Finder scoping, healing stages and the Home flag count. And the four food cards were split apart by Conditions sitting in the middle of them.

**Six groups, with headings, since the grouping is worth nothing if it is only implied:** About You, Your Health, How You Eat, Growing Your Own, How the App Looks, Device & Account. Conditions moves 4 to 2, Garden drops 2 to 8, and Diet Preferences / Meal Timing / Meal Plan / Nutrient Targets become one unbroken run.

**The headings are deliberately NOT a seventh collapse layer.** This screen already carries three (cards, TabHub icon groups, Appearance sub-sections), and a heading that can be collapsed to hide the headings under it stops being a signpost. They carry their own surface per the standing no-bare-text rule, reusing the `groupHeadingChip` shape Schedules and Trends already use for exactly this case, in the brighter primary text rather than the cards' muted label color so a group heading reads as a level above the card titles it introduces.

**Done by script rather than by hand, and the script is why it is trustworthy.** profile.tsx is ~3,700 lines and each card is a 30-to-350 line JSX block with its own preceding explanatory comment; moving those by hand is where a block gets dropped or a comment gets orphaned onto the wrong card. Every step validated before writing: block boundaries found by exact indentation then checked to hold exactly one `renderCardHeader`, blocks required to be disjoint, **the rewritten span required to contain nothing but those blocks and blank lines**, and the result required to hold the same multiset of non-blank lines as the original plus only the new heading lines. **The stray-content guard fired on the first run**, catching that comment blocks end `*/}` rather than `*/` and so were not being carried with their cards. That is the check earning its keep rather than a near miss.

`ALL_CARD_SECTION_KEYS` was realigned to the new order too. Nothing depends on it (it only seeds the all-collapsed Set and derives `CardSectionKey`), but a list disagreeing with the screen is a trap for the next reader. Verified by script that the render order and the key list match exactly, 15 cards. Developer Tools was left untouched: it has a different wrapper and was already last. `tsc` clean, `eslint` compared against HEAD and identical at 5 problems, bare-text audit 0. **Confirmed on-device: "Much better."**

**Still unconfirmed on-device, and worth saying plainly rather than letting the Profile confirmation cover the whole day:** the hands-on therapy tracker and both Digest batches (1.0.33.1 and 1.0.33.2) have shipped and been seen by nobody. The tracker is the piece most likely to hold a real problem, because it cannot be judged from one look: Therapy Response deliberately reports nothing until at least 3 sessions of the same therapy exist alongside enough check-ins on both sides to compare, so the check that matters is logging a few sessions over real days and confirming it eventually returns a day count rather than a refusal.

**Most recent (2026-09-04, 1.0.33.1): hands-on therapies, from a shared conversation that opened "I got my sacrum adjusted and now I can pee easier."** Three asks in one message: put the chiropractic-and-urine-flow material into prostate health, build a tracker for it like Bearable, and cover chiropractic, acupuncture and deep tissue massage separately across the conditions and in Basic Health.

**The source conversation's central claim was checked rather than repeated, and it splits cleanly in two.** Its anatomy is correct: the parasympathetic fibers driving the bladder leave the cord at S2 to S4 and reach it through the pelvic splanchnic nerves. Medicine takes that route seriously enough to implant a device on it, since **sacral neuromodulation of the S3 root is an established treatment** for overactive bladder and non-obstructive retention. Its mechanism claim is a different matter: a direct search for any trial of spinal manipulation or osteopathic manipulation against IPSS, maximum flow rate or post-void residual **returns nothing at all**, and the AUA guideline does not mention manipulation. That is untested rather than disproven, and the entry says so in those words. **A plausible pathway is not an answer**, which is the line the whole batch is built around.

**What does have evidence for urinary symptoms was found in the same pass**, so the entry does not end on a null. FitzGerald 2012 (PMID 22503015) is the useful one because its comparator is the interesting arm: targeted pelvic floor myofascial therapy against **global therapeutic massage**, matched for time and touch, 59% versus 26% responding. Acupuncture for chronic prostatitis has a genuinely strong trial (Sun 2021, Ann Intern Med, PMID 34399062, sustained to week 32). Acupuncture for BPH has two trials that **disagree in opposite directions**: Wang 2013 found symptoms improved while measured flow did not, Yu 2011 found flow improved while symptoms did not. Reporting both is more useful than picking one.

**The tracker is a new table rather than a fourth `treatment_type`, and that is a real distinction.** `treatments` describes a substance being taken now: dose, unit, frequency, active flag. A session is an event on a date, and the question worth asking about it is what the days AFTER it looked like, which none of those columns carry. New `therapy_sessions`, `lib/therapyTypes.ts` (13 types across 4 categories), a Schedules lens to log them, and `lib/therapyResponse.ts` plus a Trends lens to read them.

**`lib/patternFinder.ts` could not answer this question, and the reason is directional.** It looks BACKWARD from a symptom to find what preceded it. "How long did the adjustment hold" looks FORWARD from a session. So this is a second, pure analysis module rather than an extension: for each therapy it buckets check-ins by how many days after a session they fall, and compares each day against baseline.

**Four honesty gates are enforced in the module rather than left to the screen.** Nothing is reported below 3 sessions, 3 check-ins at a day offset, or 5 baseline check-ins. A day offset with too few check-ins returns a null share rather than a percentage off one entry. **The "it lasted 4 days" answer is walked as an unbroken run from day 0**, and a day with too little data breaks the run rather than being skipped, since skipping it would claim improvement across a day nothing is known about. Days that read WORSE than baseline are reported too.

**Two attribution rules are where a wrong number was easiest to produce, so both are tested directly.** A check-in is assigned to its NEAREST session, since with weekly sessions most days trail one session and precede another. And baseline is days away from a session of ANY type, not just the one being summarized: letting massage days serve as the adjustment's baseline would compare a therapy against a different therapy while calling it a baseline. `scripts/test_therapy_response.js` is 55 checks; failure output verified by removing the cross-therapy guard, which reports "expected 0, got 3" and exits non-zero.

**A bug caught by `tsc` that would have broken every launch:** the new CREATE TABLE comment used backticks around a table name, and that SQL lives inside a template literal, so the backticks terminated the string.

**Digest: 21 new entries.** A new Basic Health topic, Hands-On & Complementary Therapies (9 entries, `handson-` prefix), covering each therapy on its own terms rather than against one condition, which is what `lib/digest/complementaryTherapies.ts` already does for Hashimoto's. Six under Prostate Health, plus Migraine (2), MS (2), IBS (1) and RA (1), all on the `complementary-` prefix that `classifyConditionTopic` already routes to its own shelf, so no classifier change was needed. **Two entries report findings that do not flatter the therapies**, deliberately: Cochrane found acupuncture no better than sham for IBS, and the one deep tissue massage trial available compares massage against massage-plus-NSAID, so its design cannot show massage beat doing nothing. A topic that only ever reported these working would be an advertisement.

**New `scripts/check_related_ids.js`**, since "every new relatedIds entry confirmed to resolve" has been a hand-rolled throwaway several times in this project's history. It walks the real TypeScript AST rather than a regex over 15,000 lines of prose. It caught two ids invented from memory (`advocacy-questions-to-ask`, `advocacy-tracking-symptoms`) on its first run. Now 2,115 entries, 3,328 references, 0 problems.

`tsc` clean, `eslint` compared against the stashed tree on `schedule.tsx` and confirmed at an identical 15 problems so none are new, bare-text audit at 0, suites 30/142/29/55. **Not yet confirmed on-device**, and the checks that matter: log three sessions with check-ins around them and confirm Therapy Response reports a day count rather than a refusal; confirm the new Basic Health topic appears in the Digest menu.

**CLOSED the same day (1.0.33.2): the remaining 13 conditions, 14 more entries, all 19 now covered.** Direct follow-up: "Do the other 13 conditions." Every citation verified through the NCBI eutils endpoint rather than recalled, which caught one wrong PMID before it shipped.

**Roughly half of this batch reports that a therapy did not work**, and those are the entries worth the most. **PCOS carries the largest and best-powered trial anywhere in this whole area, and it is negative**: Wu 2017 in JAMA, 1,000 women across 27 hospitals, factorial design crossing active against sham acupuncture with clomiphene against placebo, primary outcome live birth. Live births ran 29.4% / 28.0% / 13.9% / 16.8% across the four arms. Read down that list and the clomiphene did all the work while acupuncture changed nothing in either direction, with the sham arm slightly ahead of the active one where no drug was given. **A well-powered null is worth more than a shelf of small positive studies**, which is why it leads that entry rather than being buried in a caveat.

**The clearest teaching case in the batch is cardiovascular.** A 2007 trial in the Journal of Human Hypertension reported a 17 mmHg systolic drop from one upper-neck chiropractic procedure against sham, a figure larger than most single blood pressure drugs achieve, and it is still quoted in clinics. A 2016 replication found nothing, and **it was run at the Palmer Center for Chiropractic Research on an NCCAM grant**, so it cannot be waved away as hostile. The first study was a pilot, which is what pilots are for.

**Graves' got a genuine negative rather than an absence:** a 1991 blinded study measured eye muscle volume, Hertel exophthalmometry, palpebral aperture, intraocular pressure and Hess charts after two months of acupuncture, and none of the five moved. That is a different kind of null from Hashimoto's, where a trial was designed and its results have never surfaced, and the two entries are cross-linked to make the distinction visible.

**Celiac is a flat null with `citations: []`**, following the precedent this app already set twice. There is one controlled trial of nothing, only a single case report that cannot separate acupuncture from the gluten-free diet it ran alongside.

**Two boundaries were drawn deliberately rather than inherited from the sources.** Several CKD reviews claim acupuncture improves renal function and reduces proteinuria; **those are narrative reviews, and the entry carries only what the controlled trials support**, which is fatigue and uremic pruritus in dialysis patients. And gout is where the comparison arm is the tell: trials reporting acupuncture beating colchicine and NSAIDs are claiming something implausible about drugs whose effect in an acute flare is among the most reliable in medicine, which is a reason to look harder at the trials rather than accept the result.

**The most practically useful finding is a safety fact rather than a treatment.** Massage over a recent insulin injection site speeds absorption: in one study glucose ran 8.3% lower thirty minutes later than on a control day. Heat and exercise do the same to a limb. That belongs in front of anyone with Type 1 booking a massage, and it is the whole spine of that entry, since nothing hands-on treats Type 1 itself.

Every new entry cross-links back into the Basic Health hub, and the "where acupuncture comes up empty" entry now gathers PCOS, Graves' and psoriasis alongside the IBS and migraine findings it already carried. `check_related_ids.js` caught one id invented from memory again (`celiac-depression-anxiety-comorbidity`, actually `-mental-health`). 2,129 entries, 3,385 references, 0 problems. Coverage verified by script: **19 of 19 conditions, no shelf past the 12-entry subgroup threshold.**

**Published to the `preview` EAS channel, and the reason that needs saying is that it nearly did not happen.** Both versions were committed and pushed and neither was published, until the report came in: "I don't see any new updates on eas." **This is the second time**, and the first (2026-08-30) is written up further down this same file, where the wrong answer of a stale Metro dev server was reached for before the real one. Every other item on the standing checklist was done correctly both times, which is exactly the problem: **a checklist that ends at `git push` keeps producing work that never ships.** The checklist memory now carries the publish step as item 5 rather than leaving it as folklore.

**Two mechanical details that cost time and are worth keeping.** The CLI is not installed locally or globally on this machine, and `npx eas ...` fails with "could not determine executable to run" because the binary is `eas` while the package is `eas-cli`: use `npx --yes eas-cli@latest`. Auth is a stored session in `~/.expo/state.json`, so no login is needed. And the publish output's **Runtime version came back `621e8bfc...`, byte-identical to the fingerprint of the build actually installed on both phones**, which is the compatibility check that matters and the thing the whole 2026-08-28/29 fingerprint investigation exists to make checkable.

Verified in the real exported bundle rather than assumed from a successful publish, per this project's own standing rule: `1.0.33.2`, "Hands-On Therapies", "Therapy Response", "Hands-On & Complementary Therapies", and four of the new Digest titles across both batches all confirmed present in `dist/_expo/static/js/android/*.hbc`.

**Most recent (2026-09-03, 1.0.32.18): using what the kitchen has, rather than only being told about it.** Reported directly: "There is no way to choose that you are going to take from your harvest instead of having to purchase. It is still just one selection for purchasing."

**Correct, and the kitchen inventory was half a feature without it.** Knowing a harvest covers a line is only useful if the harvest can then be used, and the whole reason `garden_harvests` and `fermentation_harvests` carry a `quantity_remaining` is so it can be drawn down as it goes. The list could say "that covers this line" and then still only offer to price it.

**Two outcomes, and the difference matters standing in a shop.** Fully covered: the harvests are drawn down by what the line needs, and the line is marked sourced from the kitchen and ticked, carrying no price because nothing was spent, so it never reaches the running total or the price history. Partly covered: the harvests are emptied, the line's quantity drops by what was taken, and it stays on the list needing the remainder, which is the honest state rather than a tick that overstates what happened.

**Allocation is oldest-harvest-first**, and each amount is converted back into that harvest's own unit, since that is what `quantity_remaining` is counted in. Proportional rather than converted a second time, so rounding cannot leave a harvest stuck at 0.0001 remaining. A purchase is never drawn down and offers no button at all: nothing tracks how much of it is left, which is exactly why it was a reminder and not an amount.

**`sourced_from_kitchen` is its own column** rather than reusing `checked`, which means "dealt with" and says nothing about how, or `price`, which stays null because nothing was spent. Added with the established conditional `ALTER TABLE` pattern, so no reference-database change and no re-import.

12 new checks on the allocation, since this decrements stored inventory and getting it wrong quietly destroys the record of what someone actually has. Failure output verified by making it take the whole harvest regardless of what the line needed: reports "expected 340, got 500" and exits non-zero. One rename on the way in, worth noting because the lint rule was right: the action was briefly `useKitchenStockForLine`, which `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` reads as a React hook. It is `takeKitchenStockForLine`.

`tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on every touched file, suites 30/142/29, bare-text audit at 0. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Most recent (2026-09-03, 1.0.32.17): test data for the kitchen sources, and a Developer Tools card that can actually be reached.** Asked for directly: "We need test data for everything in order to see what the app can or should do with it once it is in there." The app changes many times a day, so nobody is using it for real, so most of it has never run against anything. **That gap has a visible cost already**: the kitchen inventory shipped on 1.0.32.12 and has never been seen working, and three grocery bugs reached a shopping trip before anyone noticed.

**The most useful finding came before any code was written, and it is worth knowing on its own.** A seeder already exists. `lib/devSeed.ts` covers 90 days of meals, saved dishes across the builders, and food trials, with its own manifest table for exact removal. It has been gated on `__DEV__`, **which is false in an EAS build**, so it has been invisible on both phones since this app moved to standalone preview builds on 2026-08-28. Nobody could reach it. That is a large part of why so much of this app has never run against data. Now gated on `__DEV__ || Updates.channel === 'preview'`, so a testing build has it and a production build still does not.

**New `lib/testData.ts`** seeds what the kitchen inventory actually reads: a garden plot with plantings and harvests carrying `quantity_remaining`, a fermentation with a batch and a harvest, and a completed shopping trip three days old.

**It draws its foods FROM the active grocery list, and that is not a shortcut.** Matching is by exact food name, so seeding Broccoli against a list that wants Kale produces nothing on screen and the test fails for a reason that is not a bug. It also picks a unit in the same family as the line it is matching, since `kitchenCoverageFor` refuses to cross weight, volume and count, and a harvest in the wrong family is correct and invisible. The first harvest covers its line outright and the rest fall short, so both readings can be seen in one pass rather than needing two rounds of seeding.

**Kept out of devSeed's manifest deliberately:** several rows are parent/child pairs that must be deleted children-first, and that manifest is walked in insertion order, which is parents-first. Rather than make one list carry a constraint it was never built for, each module removes its own rows in its own order and reports the count. One Clear button, two modules each responsible for what they created.

**Home says so while any test data is loaded**, above the loading gate (whether test data is present is true regardless of what has finished fetching) and deliberately not a toggleable Home section, since a warning that can be switched off stops being a warning.

`tsc` clean, `eslint` clean on both new and touched lib files (`profile.tsx` and `index.tsx` at their pre-existing 6, confirmed against the stashed tree), suites 30/130/29, bare-text audit at 0. **Confirmed on-device 2026-09-05: "I checked the the seeding and it works fine."** That also closes the older gap this work existed to fix: the kitchen inventory, shipped 1.0.32.12 and unseen until now, has finally been exercised against data. Phases 2 and 3 (logged history plus symptoms; saved dishes plus schedule) are named and not started, though devSeed's own 90-day seeder already covers much of both and is now reachable for the first time.

**Most recent (2026-09-03, 1.0.32.16): the app says what the TabHub button is.** Reported through a first-time reader of the app, and correct: the button that reaches all nine tabs does not look like a button. Confirmed in the code rather than taken on faith. It carries **no circle, no fill, no border and no label at rest**, deliberately (`components/TabHub.tsx`: "the artwork itself is the button"), and its only description, "Open navigation menu", exists for screen readers alone. To someone who has never opened this app it is a drawing of a seed at the bottom of the screen, with every tool in the app behind it.

**The asymmetry that made this easy to miss:** the SECONDARY hub already introduces itself. `GatedTabContent` renders a resting prompt on every tab saying to tap the corner button (added 1.0.31.15, when the LensHub menus stopped opening themselves). The primary hub, the one that moves between tabs at all, said nothing anywhere, and no first-run onboarding existed in the app at all.

**Two pieces, in the order asked for.** A welcome shown once ever, dimming the screen and leaving the button lit, so the first thing anyone sees is the thing to press.
