**(2) "The meals you can eat should be separated into groups specific to what they are, such as related to the Food builders that they would open into."** Confirmed real: "Meals You Can Eat" was one flat, unbroken shelf of up to 300 recipes per condition, with no way to jump straight to, say, just the sides. Fixed by reusing the exact same classification the plain Recipes category already uses for its own topic menu (`classifyRecipesTopic`/`RECIPES_TOPIC_ORDER`: Sides, Salads & Bowls, Smoothies, Fermentation, Beverages, Snacks, Baked Goods, Soups, Sauces, Handhelds, Desserts), so a recipe's own sub-group here always matches the exact Food builder it would actually open into. `groupConditionEntries` now emits one real `'::'`-joined sub-topic per non-empty builder type under the "Meals You Can Eat" label (`Meals You Can Eat::Sides`, and so on) instead of one flat bucket, the same real nesting convention Essential Nutrients' own 22 subtopics already established -- `shelfHeadingLabel`'s existing `::`-stripping logic needed zero changes to display each one correctly. Within each sub-shelf, the same clean-first-then-cautioned priority order from the two prior sessions' own work is preserved exactly, since entries are bucketed in the order they already arrive in, never independently re-sorted.

Picking "Meals You Can Eat" from a condition's own top-level topic menu now shows every one of its own non-empty sub-shelves stacked together at once (Sides, Salads & Bowls, and so on, each independently horizontally scrollable), not a further click-through subtopic menu the way Essential Nutrients requires -- a deliberate, scoped choice: at most 12 sub-groups here (fewer than Essential Nutrients' 22, the case that specifically needed an extra menu step to stay fast), and every shelf is already virtualized (the 2026-08-23 `FlatList` fix), so the same performance concern that drove Essential Nutrients' own extra step doesn't apply here at the same severity. The top-level topic menu itself still shows exactly one "Meals You Can Eat" row with a real, correctly summed total count, via a new, generic `collapseTopicsForMenu` helper (mirroring `basicHealthMenuGroups`' own established collapsing technique, order-preserving rather than alphabetized, matching this generic path's own "keep each category's curated order" rule).

**Two real regressions caught and fixed before shipping, not after:** the two category-scoped search useMemos (`categorySearchScopeEntries`, `categorySearchGroups`) both used to resolve "Meals You Can Eat" via an exact label match, which would have silently found nothing once the label became several `'::'`-joined sub-topics instead of one flat string, one falling back to searching the WHOLE category instead of just this one topic, the other returning zero results outright. Both fixed the same way `BasicHealthShelves`' own drill-in filter was, matching on the label's own top-level segment (`label.split('::')[0]`) rather than requiring an exact match, combining every matching sub-topic's own entries.

`tsc` clean project-wide, `eslint` clean on the one touched file. No Digest content changed, so no `PURPLE_DIGEST_VERSION` bump; `APP_VERSION` bumped to 1.0.26.1 (day segment 26, a new calendar day). **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Most recent (2026-08-24): "Meals You Can Eat" fixed from a hard gate into a real advisory list, across all 19 conditions.** Direct report: "I looked at meals you can eat in Hashimoto's and it literally only has a bunch of fermented drinks listed... they are far from being meals... What they can eat is exactly that, everything they can eat, at the levels of healing that they need to start from and achieve along the way." Confirmed by direct count before writing any code: Hashimoto's own "safe" list was 18 of 300 recipes, every single one a fermented drink (yogurt, kombucha, kefir, kvass, and so on), zero actual meals.

**Root cause.** The feature's original build (shipped a few hours earlier the same day) used `safeForConditions` as a hard include/exclude gate: a recipe was shown only if ZERO of its ingredients tripped ANY flag relevant to that condition. Combined with a wide criteria net (Hashimoto's owns 25 real relevant sub-criteria, the most of any condition), more ingredients meant more chances to trip one single flag somewhere, so only near-single-ingredient recipes could ever pass. This also directly contradicted this app's own standing healing-stage rule, already established for individual foods (`lib/foodStageReordering.ts`): "advisory and reordering only, never gating." A direct count across the other 18 conditions confirmed the same underlying defect at different severities: Psoriasis/Rheumatoid Arthritis (81/300), Cardiovascular Disease (84/300), Lupus/MS/Sjögren's (107/300 each) were all meaningfully thin; 10 of the 19 conditions already sat near 300/300 and weren't practically affected.

**The fix.** `safeForConditions` (a recipe with zero relevant flags) is kept, but no longer excludes anything -- `scripts/compute_recipe_condition_data.js` now also computes a new `conditionCautions: {conditionCode: string}` per recipe: for every condition where a recipe IS flagged, a real, computed one-sentence caution naming the single most severe flagged ingredient (red before yellow) and what the flag means, built from the same tier vocabulary `lib/sixDimensionsReference.ts` already uses everywhere else in this app (e.g. "Whole-Grain Wheat Flour: rated High Risk for gluten. A significant, well-documented concern."). A first version made the flagged ingredient's own name the grammatical subject of a verb and broke on subject-verb agreement for any plural ingredient ("Flax seeds skews..."); fixed by restructuring to a colon-plus-explanation form that needs no agreement at all.

"Meals You Can Eat" now shows every recipe with real per-condition data for that condition, genuinely clean ones first, flagged ones after, each carrying its own specific caution once opened from that condition's own page -- never excluded, matching the app's own advisory-only rule instead of contradicting it. New `RecipeCard.conditionCautions?: Record<string, string>` (`lib/digest/types.ts`). A new, deliberately separate `scripts/apply_recipe_condition_cautions.js` writes it into `recipes.ts` (kept apart from the original `apply_recipe_condition_data.js`, whose own `conditionNotes`-appending logic is already known not to be idempotent, per the Migraine entry below -- this new script only ever fully overwrites its own field, verified idempotent by running it three times and confirming zero diff after the first application). The caution itself is threaded through as a new `activeConditionCode` prop (`BasicHealthShelves` -> `DigestCard` -> `RecipeCardDetail`), rendered in its own distinct "A note for this condition" box, deliberately kept separate from the always-visible "Worth knowing if you have..." box (`conditionNotes`) rather than folded into it -- stuffing a mechanically generated caution for all 19 conditions into that box on every recipe would have buried the real, hand-written notes already there.

**Same-day direct follow-up: "Now factor in their declared healing stage too."** Closes the named gap above. For the 6 conditions with a real healing-stage model, "Meals You Can Eat" now uses the person's own Profile-declared stage two ways: within the flagged/cautioned group, a recipe with a real stage-specific advisory hit for their CURRENT stage now sorts behind ones that don't (so "worth a look right now" leads over "a concern for later"), and the recipe's own detail view prefers the richer, stage-specific note (already computed back when the feature first shipped, `stageAdvisoryNotes`) over the plain per-condition caution when one exists for that exact stage. No declared stage, or a condition with no real staging model, leaves everything exactly as the same-day fix above already left it.

**A real, higher-impact bug found and fixed along the way, not assumed correct from a passing type-check:** the stage labels the original build hand-typed into its own `STAGED_CONDITIONS` list (`compute_recipe_condition_data.js`) had drifted from the real, canonical stage labels Profile's own stage picker actually shows (`lib/conditionStages.ts` and each condition's own `*_STAGE_INFO`/`*_PHASE_INFO`): Hashimoto's "Digging (Removing Triggers)"/"Gut Repair (Reintroduction)" should have been "Stage 2: Digging"/"Stage 3: Gut Repair", Gout's "Acute Flare"/"Intercritical (Between Flares)" should have carried the same "Stage N:" prefix, and IBS's "Elimination Phase" should have been "Phase 1: Elimination." Caught only because building the new stage-aware lookup against the REAL canonical labels (not the drifted ones) surfaced a silent zero-match. This wasn't just an internal lookup problem: the mismatched label text was already being shown directly to users in every recipe's own "Worth knowing if you have..." box since the feature first shipped a few hours earlier the same day, so this fix also corrects real, already-visible copy, not only the new sort/caution logic. Fixed at the source (the compute script's own labels, so any future regeneration stays correct) and, separately, with a precise, verified string replacement directly against the already-applied text in `recipes.ts` (350 lines changed, exactly matching the combined count of the two affected labels, confirmed via `git diff --stat` before trusting it) -- deliberately not by re-running the original `apply_recipe_condition_data.js`, whose own `conditionNotes`-appending logic is already known not to be idempotent. Gout's own mismatch had zero practical impact to fix in `recipes.ts` itself: this app's own curated recipes never trip Gout's narrow Additives/Processing-only stage trigger at all (0 real stage notes generated for Gout, confirmed directly), so there was nothing already written to correct, only the script's own labels for going forward.

**Most recent (2026-08-24): a corpus-wide sweep for genuinely truncated, unfinished sentences across the Digest, 6 real instances found and fixed.** Direct report, quoting the exact broken text: "The research elsewhere is almost entirely about whether a given food helps or hurts a specific condition, assuming the food itself is." -- a sentence that just stops mid-thought. A scripted sweep of every `summary`/`teaser`/`note`/`relevanceNote`/`stageNote`/`mechanism`/`problem` field across all 61 `lib/digest/*.ts` files found 5 more genuine cutoffs beyond the one reported (`choosingQualityProducts.ts`, `foodAdditives.ts`, `problemFoods.ts`, `selfAdvocacy.ts`, `lifestyleEnvironment.ts`, one inside `foodIndustryHistory.ts`'s own AI-opinion-synthesis entry). Each fixed by reading the full entry to reconstruct what the sentence was actually building toward, not deleted or patched with a placeholder.

**Same-day direct correction to the sweep above: the "grammatically legal" bar the first pass used was itself wrong.** The first pass's own report used "the mechanism celiac disease was the original research population for." as an example of a sentence it correctly left alone, grammatically complete via preposition-stranding. Direct pushback, quoting that exact sentence back: "is not a complete sentence. For me it has no beginning or end... if it doesn't make sense when they read it, then there is no point to writing the app at all." Correct: formal grammatical legality was never the actual bar. The real bar is whether an average reader parses a sentence cleanly on one pass without mentally rearranging it, and that sentence buries its own antecedent a full clause before the stranded "for," forcing exactly that kind of backtracking even though a strict parse defends it.

Re-reading the same candidate list under the corrected standard found 10 more real problems the first pass's grammar-only check had waved through, across 8 files (`celiac.ts`, `bodyFatBiology.ts`, `bodySystems.ts`, `essentialNutrients.ts`, `gutMicrobiome.ts`, `ibs.ts`, `cardiovascularDisease.ts`, `foodIndustryHistory.ts`): the reported celiac sentence itself, rewritten to state its own antecedent before the reference to it rather than stranding a preposition behind a whole intervening clause; two more of the same long-distance-stranding shape (`bodyFatBiology.ts`, `bodySystems.ts`); one elided verb that read as incomplete ("...who actually needs to." fixed to name what: "...needs to supplement in the first place"); one ellipsis needing a real predicate ("...the connection is." to "...the connection holds up"); and, caught in the same close-reading pass though not part of the original report, a garbled word ("cefor instance" to "cereal, for instance"), two "a/an" agreement errors ("A honest complication" to "An honest"), one subject-verb agreement error ("practices there is" to "there are"), and one stray comma splitting an adjective from its noun. The same sweep, run a second time across `app/**/*.tsx` and `components/*.tsx` as directly requested ("Run the same sweep across the rest of the app's screen text"), came back genuinely clean: every flagged candidate was confirmed on full reading to be a natural, complete sentence, or a scanner artifact from JSX text split across sibling `{...}` expressions, not real broken text. A real scanner bug was caught and fixed along the way: the first script's naive quote-matching was snagging on apostrophes inside `//` comments and consuming to the next stray quote mark, producing 73 garbage hits; a corrected version that strips comments while respecting real string-literal boundaries brought that down to 10 candidates, all confirmed legitimate. Standing writing-style memory updated with this corrected standard (`feedback_writing_style.md`). `tsc`/`eslint` clean across all 8 touched files. **Not yet confirmed on-device** (pure text changes, same low visual risk as the first pass).

A real, hard-won detection lesson: a naive "flag any sentence ending on a word that can't end a sentence" heuristic produced 783 false-positive-dominated hits on the first pass, since this app's own prose style leans heavily on legitimate preposition-stranding relative clauses ("the mechanism celiac disease was the original research population for.") and elliptical short sentences completing via the prior one ("Sometimes it is."). The one signal that actually held up: a sentence ending on a bare linking verb (is/was/are/were) or article/possessive determiner with literally nothing after it -- no legitimate stranding explanation exists for those, unlike a preposition. A second check confirmed zero fields anywhere in the corpus are missing terminal punctuation entirely. Scope named honestly: this sweep covered `lib/digest/*.ts` specifically, not the rest of the app's UI copy.

**Most recent (2026-08-24): AIP diet and migraine researched, 2 new Digest entries.** Direct request: "I think migraines probably could be related to the AIP diet in reduction of inflamation as it would pertain to the brain. Research that and any study about that which could be used in this app and provide real solid data." The honest finding, stated directly rather than glossed over: no published trial has tested the Autoimmune Protocol itself on migraine, a real, named gap in the current literature (which explicitly lists migraine as a future AIP research direction, not a settled one).

What real evidence does exist, covered in two new entries in `lib/digest/migraine.ts`: (1) a 2025 randomized, sham-controlled trial (98 adults, PMID 41473187) testing the same underlying mechanism AIP is built on, food elimination to calm systemic inflammation, found statistically significant drops in IL-6, TNF-alpha, and CGRP itself (the neuropeptide behind an actual migraine attack, already covered in this category's own trigeminovascular entry), plus fewer migraine days and lower MIDAS severity scores; a separate 2024 review (PMID 39064664) names the real pathway connecting gut-level food elimination to brain-level effect, increased intestinal permeability letting inflammatory molecules into systemic circulation, where they directly stimulate the trigeminovascular system. (2) A distinct, real mechanism AIP's own elimination list also touches without being designed around it: 87% of migraine patients show measurable DAO enzyme deficiency versus 44% of controls (PMID 28624934, p<0.0001), impairing the body's ability to break down dietary histamine, one of the foods AIP eliminates (fermented foods, aged cheese, cured meats) being independently histamine-rich; a separate randomized trial of DAO enzyme supplementation (PMID 30017233) found a real reduction in headache burden, confirming the pathway is causal, not just correlational.

Both entries tiered `moderate` (real, controlled-trial-level evidence for the underlying mechanisms, not direct trial evidence for AIP itself, an honest distinction named directly in both entries' own text). Cross-linked to the existing `diet-aip` Basic Health entry, `migraine-trigeminovascular-cgrp-mechanism`, `migraine-food-triggers-honest-nuance`, and `migraine-fermented-drinks`, each of those updated with a reverse link too. A real writing-style self-check caught and fixed 6 instances of overused "real"/"honest" filler and 3 instances of the redundant "X's own Y" pattern in the first draft before shipping, confirmed clean by direct grep, not assumed from a passing `tsc`.

**A real, concrete follow-up this research opens up, named directly rather than acted on unprompted:** Migraine currently has zero real condition-scoped food-scoring data in the reference database, which is why it was excluded from the "Meals You Can Eat" feature shipped earlier the same day. The Additives/Processing sub-criteria already exist and are already reused by other conditions via `sub_criterion_condition_relevance` -- a real, defensible relevance mapping for Migraine (Additives/Processing, matching the histamine/inflammatory-trigger mechanism just researched) could extend that same feature to a 19th condition. Not built in this pass; a real, scoped next step if wanted.

**Two real bugs caught and fixed before shipping.** First: "Selenium & Zn synergy" and "Iron Presence" tiers hit roughly 50% and 5.5% of all 22,022 foods respectively, a known near-universal background signal this app's own recipes.ts header comment already documents excluding from hand-written cautions -- excluded here the same way. **Most recent (2026-08-24): chrononutrition research content shipped, phase 3 of 3 of the same larger request (chrononutrition reorg → diet tracks → research content), all three phases now complete.** Direct follow-up, after the vegan/vegetarian tracks below shipped: "Keep going straight into the research content now."

**New `lib/digest/chrononutrition.ts`, a Basic Health topic with 9 entries**, covering the actual science: the master clock (SCN) versus peripheral clocks in the liver/gut/pancreas and why food, not light, synchronizes the peripheral ones; the diurnal insulin-sensitivity rhythm behind the "dawn phenomenon"; early time-restricted eating's real RCT evidence (Sutton 2018); an honest complication where a real T2D trial found glucose control improved but insulin sensitivity itself didn't; the NutriNet-Santé cohort linking late eating to cardiovascular risk; the gut microbiome's own diurnal rhythm (Thaiss 2014); shift work as a real-world natural experiment in circadian disruption. Two claims got a direct, honest correction rather than being repeated as settled fact, per the source conversation's own framing: the popular claim that eating late "blocks autophagy" turns out genuinely mixed in human research (a 2024 study found no acute change from one meal, a 2025 study found a longer-term intervention may increase autophagic flux, not the same thing); and the specific "cortisol awakening response" mechanism has a real, recent complication (newer research found no evidence of an increased rate of cortisol secretion specifically in the hour after waking), separate from the broader morning-peak cortisol rhythm, which remains solid.

**19 new condition-specific entries, one per tracked condition**, each independently researched and cited, not template-filled: Hashimoto's and Graves' (circadian clock gene disruption in autoimmune thyroiditis, BMAL1/PER2 reduced in affected thyroid tissue); Rheumatoid Arthritis (the CAPRA-1 trial, real chronotherapy, timing a prednisone dose to the overnight IL-6 peak measurably shortened morning stiffness); Type 1 Diabetes (the dawn phenomenon's real clinical magnitude, 58-66% higher insulin need); Type 2 Diabetes (a genuine TRE nuance, cross-linked to an existing entry rather than duplicated, see below); Celiac and IBD (clock gene disruption in inflamed gut tissue, an active, not-yet-settled research direction); Multiple Sclerosis and Lupus and Sjögren's (melatonin/BMAL1/salivary-gland clock genes, each a real but still-mechanistic finding, tiered accordingly); PCOS (a real 6-month RCT where time-restricted eating lowered a marker of excess androgen that calorie restriction alone didn't); Chronic Kidney Disease (nocturnal blood-pressure non-dipping, a real circadian-biology finding distinct from meal timing, named honestly as such); Fatty Liver Disease (the liver's own clock and why irregular eating tracks with MASLD risk); IBS (night shift work linked to a real jump in IBS-like symptoms); Migraine (a striking real finding, 110 of 168 migraine susceptibility genes are circadian clock genes); Cardiovascular Disease (the same NutriNet-Santé cohort, condition-specific framing); Gout (the real mechanism behind gout's well-known nocturnal flare pattern, NLRP3 inflammasome circadian control); Prostate Health (nocturnal polyuria's real vasopressin/melatonin mechanism); Psoriasis (skin's own circadian clock and the F3 gene's role in IL-17 signaling).

**The real gap an audit found, wider than the direct report itself named:** not just the 6 Smoothies (all clustered at the very start of the plan, days 1-6, which is what made it feel more frequent than its true 6-of-42 rate), but 13 more breakfasts -- every overnight-oats, warm-porridge, and chia-pudding recipe -- used almond or coconut milk as their own liquid base, carrying almost no protein and no fermented element either. All 19 fixed the same way: swapped to a real Greek yogurt base (new `scripts/chrononutrition_breakfast_protein_boost.py`, patching both the live database and matching `lib/digest/recipes.ts` entries), adding real protein and making the breakfast itself a fermented food. Three "coconut"-named recipes keep half their coconut milk rather than a full swap, so the flavor the name promises stays real; the two warm porridges keep a reduced amount of almond milk for the actual cooking liquid and get the yogurt stirred in as a real finishing step instead, since yogurt heated directly in a simmering pot tends to split. Every added honey amount was made optional rather than removed outright -- a small amount of real honey next to a large amount of whole fruit isn't the processed "hidden sugar" the research is actually warning against, but making it optional still honors the direct instruction that sugar doesn't belong in breakfast by default. Every one of the 42 breakfasts now has a real protein anchor (egg, yogurt, or cottage cheese); none did before.

**Separately, 6 days (9, 10, 17, 34, 36, 42) had their lunch and dinner swapped**, no new recipes needed: each one's dinner slot held a dedicated grain (brown rice, wild rice, or couscous) while its own lunch was already a lighter, grain-free salad or soup. Real evidence points the other way -- insulin sensitivity is highest earlier in the day, and a lighter, lower-starch dinner eaten well before bed is associated with better cardiometabolic outcomes in a real 103,000-person cohort (NutriNet-Santé, Nature Communications 2023). Whole-food starchy vegetables at dinner (potato, sweet potato, parsnip, turnip) were deliberately left alone rather than swapped, treated as a real, fiber-rich food, not the same concern as a dedicated refined-grain side.

Please go through this entire app's writings and make sure the word is appropriately used and not AI used." Scale check done first: 2,854 raw "'s own"/"its own"/"their own" matches across `lib/digest/*.ts` alone. A blind find-replace was ruled out directly, since some uses carry actual meaning (the "in its own right"/"on its own terms" idiom family, the standalone "on X's own" meaning "independently," and this app's own legitimate autoimmune-disease framing, "the immune system attacks the body's own tissue," where "own" carries meaningful self-versus-foreign medical distinction). A scripted, staged pass instead: a Node script skipping code comments entirely (only customer-facing `title`/`teaser`/`summary`/`stageNote` text touched) and skipping any removal where the possessor was animate/personal (body, person, someone, patient, mother, wife, gut, immune, thyroid) or the following word was body/tissue-related, run in dry-run first, spot-checked, then applied.

Two distinct bugs caught only by careful post-apply auditing, not assumed clean from a passing type-check alone: first, the script's regex required a literal apostrophe, silently missing every instance inside a single-quoted string using an escaped apostrophe (`glyphosate\'s own`), a second pass with a corrected regex caught 366 more, including the exact glyphosate example quoted in the request. Second, stripping "own" from the "on its own [verb]" idiom (meaning "independently") left broken grammar in a small number of cases ("on its own does not" losing "own" and "does not" both) since the word right after "own" was a verb, not a noun; a systematic, three-tier verification (a narrow verb/conjunction stopword list checked against re-derived original text, a broader idiom-noun restoration for "right"/"terms"/"merits", and a "deserves/worth its own coverage" template restoration run twice after a second pass re-broke it once) found and fixed all instances, confirmed by a final zero-result sweep. `tsc` clean project-wide, `eslint` clean across all 58 touched files, zero "own own" duplicates, the exact quoted example confirmed fixed. Standing writing-style rule updated to cover this going forward. **Not yet confirmed on-device** (a pure text change, low visual risk, but not yet read through by a human on the actual app).

5 new Basic Health entries in `lib/digest/mentalHealth.ts`: ultra-processed food intake and depression/anxiety risk (a 2022 meta-analysis of 385,541 people, 44% higher odds of depressive symptoms and 48% higher odds of anxiety symptoms at the highest intake level, honestly flagged as observational, not causal, and cross-checked against a second meta-analysis that found the depression link but not the anxiety one, a disagreement reported rather than smoothed over); the actual gut-microbiome-to-mood mechanism (fiber fermented into short-chain fatty acids, not serotonin transport, with the blood-brain-barrier correction named directly and cross-linked to IBS's own existing, and separately accurate, gut-serotonin-motility entry); blood sugar instability and insulin resistance as a shared mood mechanism; vitamin D and depression (honestly tiered as a mixed, evolving evidence base, explicitly not overriding this Digest's own existing conservative supplementation guidance); and magnesium/zinc deficiency and mood.

**The greeting card.** New `greetingCardState`, a plain `'initial' | 'collapsed' | 'expanded'` piece of session state, not a saved preference. `'initial'`: full size, in normal document flow, unchanged from before, for 60 seconds after Home first mounts (a plain `useEffect` timer, not `useFocusEffect`, so it fires once per app open, not every tab switch back to Home, since Home stays mounted across tab switches). Then `'collapsed'`: the card leaves document flow entirely (everything below it moves up to fill the space, exactly as asked) and a small floating seed badge, pinned at the top left of `contentArea` (already positioned below `ScreenHeader`, so no separate safe-area math was needed), takes its place as a sibling of the ScrollView, the same "floats over the scrollable content" technique this screen's own `bottomMask`/`EdgeShadow` already use. Tapping it goes to `'expanded'`: the full card again, at the same top-left origin so it visibly grows back out of the badge, floating over the already-moved-up content rather than back in document flow, at a modest `opacity: 0.92` (background and text together, deliberately mild since every text style already carries its own `textShadow`) so it reads as temporary. A second `useEffect`, keyed on `greetingCardState` itself, auto-collapses it again after 30 seconds, cleared early if the badge itself is tapped first.

The badge is the same `seed-tall-transparent.png` the TabHub button's own default icon already uses, not new art, appearing in three places with one shared render function: the corner of the full card in both `'initial'` and `'expanded'` (tap to collapse), and standing alone as the whole of `'collapsed'` (tap to expand). A bug caught before shipping: the first version hardcoded the badge's own tap to always collapse, which would have made the standalone collapsed badge do nothing when tapped (already collapsed). Fixed with an `action: 'collapse' | 'expand'` parameter instead of one fixed behavior.

**Reordering.** New `homeSectionOrder: HomeSectionKey[]` on `VisualPreferences`, following the same "absence means default" contract `homeSectionVisibility` already established, reconciled through a new `getOrderedHomeSectionKeys()` rather than read directly, so a saved order missing a section added to Home later still shows that section (appended in its own designed position) instead of silently hiding it. New `REORDERABLE_HOME_SECTION_KEYS`, `ALL_HOME_SECTION_KEYS` minus `'weather'`, derived rather than hand-duplicated: the welcome box itself was never a `HomeSectionKey` to begin with, and `weather` specifically renders embedded inside that same fixed box, not as an independent section, so excluding it from reordering was already implied by the existing architecture, not a new exception invented for this request.

Profile's own "Home Screen" card gained a new "Order" list below the existing visibility toggles: one row per reorderable section, up and down buttons rather than drag-and-drop (no drag library exists in this project yet, and a plain tap matches the low-risk-control convention every other picker on this screen already follows). Home's own render logic was restructured to match: the 9 reorderable sections, each already a self-contained block of JSX, were pulled into their own functions (`renderSymptomCheckinReminder`, `renderTodaysCheckin`, etc., every one unchanged from its own prior JSX, just relocated) and dispatched through one `renderHomeSection(key)` switch, called in whatever order `getOrderedHomeSectionKeys()` returns rather than a sequence hardcoded into the JSX itself. `digestCards` (the Digest flip cards), which used to render outside the loading gate the other 8 sections wait on, was folded into the same gate here: once any section can land anywhere in the order, one section skipping that gate wherever it happened to land would leave a real, confusing gap in the middle of the sequence while neighboring sections are still waiting, a deliberate, named simplification, not an oversight.

Investigating (1) surfaced a gap: Home's "A Few Things Worth Knowing" flip cards were never actually Digest-sourced despite the name, a fixed, hand-written array of 17 Hashimoto's/autoimmune tidbits, unrelated to which conditions someone actually has. Rebuilt as `digestFlipCardPool()`, a live filter over `ALL_DIGEST_ENTRIES` scoped to `basicHealth` (the free-tier content) plus the person's own selected conditions, memoized so filtering 1,500+ entries only recomputes when that scope actually changes. New `curious_about_conditions` table (`lib/db.ts`), deliberately separate from `user_conditions`, same shape, so nothing that reads the tracked-conditions table (scoring, medication rules, healing stages) ever sees a condition someone is merely curious about. New Profile sub-section, "Curious about other conditions," same `conditionGrid` pill layout as the existing picker, filtered to exclude whatever's already selected as one's own; selecting a condition as one's own also clears it from curious-about automatically, so the same condition never shows pinned in both lists. `CONDITION_CODE_TO_DIGEST_KEY` (already shared with Digest's own LensHub pinning) bridges the reference database's snake_case condition codes to this app's camelCase Digest categories. `ProblemFoodEntry`-shaped Digest entries (no `title`/`summary` of their own) are handled via the existing `isProblemFoodEntry` type guard rather than assumed away. Per-entry icons are gone (the old array hand-picked a different Ionicons glyph per tidbit); every card now uses `PurpleRibbonIcon`, tying each one visibly back to where it came from.

(2) and (3): audited `app/(tabs)/index.tsx` directly rather than guessed. Found 12 text styles using a `typography` preset with no `textShadow` at all (the sky-data grid, `CardLabel`, the periodic-assessment-due banner, all of Today's Check-In's own internal text) and added it to each. Found the border width actually had two tiers already, `TAB_BORDER_WIDTH` (2px) for boxes whose border color is dynamically set to a tab identity color, and a plain 1px for smaller controls (buttons, pills, chips, the text input), which were each already internally consistent. The actual inconsistency was 3 cards (`loadingCard`, `allSectionsHiddenCard`, `greetingCard`) left at the old 1px specifically because their border carries no tab-color meaning, a reasoned distinction at the time it was made, but one that read as visual inconsistency once actually seen next to every other card on the same screen. Moved all 3 to `TAB_BORDER_WIDTH`, and `moreFlipCard`'s own already-matching hardcoded `2` now references the same shared constant. `TAB_BORDER_WIDTH`'s own comment updated in place to explain the current, correct reasoning rather than leave the superseded one standing.

`tsc` clean project-wide; `eslint` clean on every touched file (2 new unescaped-apostrophe issues introduced by this pass's own new Profile text were caught and fixed; several more pre-existing ones elsewhere in `profile.tsx`/`index.tsx`, unrelated to this change, confirmed via `git diff` and left untouched). Five files touched (`app/(tabs)/index.tsx`, `app/profile.tsx`, `lib/db.ts` new table plus 2 new functions). **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Most recent (2026-08-23): a disk-space audit, direct request, "scan the entire build of the app looking for unnecessary code or notes or anything that adds to bloating the app."** Measured rather than guessed: `du` across every top-level folder, `git ls-files` to separate what's actually tracked from local-only build output, `git count-objects`/`.git/lfs` inspection for repository history size, and a cross-reference of every image in `assets/` against every `require()` in the source tree.

**Fixed outright, zero risk, git-tracked and confirmed dead:** 17 files, roughly 8.4MB. Nine `.bak`/`.bak2`/`.bak3` snapshots left over from the icon-redesign work (`icon.png`, `android-icon-foreground.png`, `android-icon-monochrome.png`, each backed up 3 times, none ever read by any config or `require()`), 2 more (`seed-transparent.png.bak`/`.bak2`) backing up a file that was already deleted outright back on 2026-08-21, 2 confirmed-unreferenced background images (`App_Background_Image.png`, `Fruits_Vegetables.png`, both explicitly superseded and left in place at the time per this document's own 2026-08-21/22 entries), and 4 unused default Expo template assets (`react-logo.png` and its `@2x`/`@3x` variants, `partial-react-logo.png`, confirmed against every `.tsx`/`.ts`/`.json` file in the project, `splash-icon.png` is the one template image actually still wired into `app.json` and was left alone). Every one of these already has its full history preserved in git regardless, so nothing is actually lost.

**Named, not touched, because each one needs a deliberate decision rather than a safe default:**
- `.git`'s own local size is 2.0GB, and 1.8GB of that is the local git-lfs object cache holding 13 historical versions of the two tracked databases (`foods_reference.db`, `unified_foods.sqlite`). `git lfs prune` would reclaim most of that safely (it only drops local cache copies still recoverable from the LFS remote), but it's an operation on repository state, not something to run unprompted.
- `android/` is 2.1GB of local native build output, entirely untracked by git, regenerates automatically on the next native build. Safe to delete for disk space, at the cost of a rebuild next time one is needed.
- `ClaudeWork/` is 267MB of raw source-data downloads and early build scripts from the original database-building work in mid-July (national nutrition datasets, an old `build_food_database.py` v1/v2/v3, even a duplicate copy of one .zip download), untracked, and not read by the actual production pipeline (`scripts/build_food_reference_db.py` reads from a different OneDrive folder entirely). Looks disposable, not confirmed disposable, since some of these downloads could be hard to re-fetch if ever needed again.
- `unified-database/` (254MB) and `node_modules/` (3.8GB) are both expected, both explained elsewhere in this document, neither is bloat to fix.

**On the comments themselves**, since "unnecessary... notes" was named directly: this codebase's own header-comment convention (the detailed build-journal style visible throughout `lib/`, `scripts/`, and this document) does not bloat the shipped app. Metro's production bundler strips comments during minification, so none of this reaches an installed phone; the only cost is source-repository size, and plain text compresses efficiently in git, a small cost next to the LFS history above. Not changed, and not treated as the same category of problem the asset backups were.

`tsc` clean project-wide after the deletions (nothing in code referenced any of the 17 removed files, confirming the audit's own cross-reference was accurate before anything was deleted). **Confirmable on-device only in the negative: nothing should look different, since none of the removed files were ever shown to begin with.**

**Also 2026-08-23: a new Earth Matters topic, Climate Science & the Weather Machine, built from a 2019 NOVA documentary the user is currently watching.** Direct request: "I am now watching a documentary from 2019 called Decoding the weather machine. This data is part of the Inside Story of our planet and belongs in the Earth Matters area. Research everything about the topics discussed in this documentation, branch from it to determine what is up to date now about all of that data and create a place, if it doesn't already exist, where this data deserves to be." No place for climate science existed in Earth Matters before this: its 10 existing topics are entirely about the organic/regenerative-agriculture movement.

New `lib/digest/climateScience.ts`, 10 entries, none sourced from the documentary's own footage or narration: every entry traces to the agency page, satellite record, or peer-reviewed study the film's own segment is actually built on, individually verified via WebSearch, each explicitly checked for what has changed since the film's 2019 vantage point. The greenhouse effect mechanism and the Mauna Loa CO2 record (NASA, NOAA, Scripps) anchor the batch; the ice-core paleoclimate record the film describes as reaching roughly 800,000 years is updated to the January 2025 Beyond EPICA announcement reaching 1.2 million; climate model reliability cites the Hausfather 2020 verification study plus NASA GISS's own confirmation; extreme weather attribution science, still young in 2019, is shown matured into a repeatable, partly peer-reviewed World Weather Attribution methodology; global temperature status cites the WMO's own 2025 State of the Global Climate report (2015-2025 the eleven warmest years on record). Three entries branch beyond what the film covers at all: satellite-measured sea level rise acceleration and GRACE/GRACE-FO polar ice sheet mass loss (the direct physical consequence side of the film's own hurricane/drought segments), the Armstrong McKay 2022 Science synthesis on climate tipping-point risk (a term the film uses without quantifying), and renewable energy's own cost and deployment growth since 2019 via the IEA's 2025 renewables report, the mitigation side of the story the film's own closing segment has no numbers for.

Every entry carries an honestly tiered evidence level, not a blanket "strong": the ice-core age is confirmed but its full climate record is still under analysis (tiered `moderate`), individual rapid attribution studies are released before full peer review even though the underlying method is peer-reviewed (`moderate`), tipping-point thresholds are named consequences of well-established mechanisms but their specific timing carries acknowledged uncertainty (`moderate`), and the renewable-energy forecast is itself a moving target, the IEA's own 2025 figure is a downward revision from its 2024 one (`moderate`). Wired into `purple-digest.tsx` as a new `EarthMattersTopic` ("Climate Science & the Weather Machine," placed right after the soil-science lead as the category's other planetary-systems foundation) with its own `id.startsWith('climate-')` classification rule, and into `lib/digest/index.ts`'s entry list. A first pass, named honestly, not exhaustive: this is a two-hour documentary built around dozens of named scientists and field locations, and this batch covers its core scientific throughlines with current, individually verified sourcing rather than reconstructing every scene. `tsc`/`eslint` clean, three files touched (`lib/digest/climateScience.ts` new, `lib/digest/index.ts`, `purple-digest.tsx`). **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Also 2026-08-23: a standing writing-style violation identified and a large first pass removed across the whole Digest content base.** Direct report, quoting "A honest limitation worth stating plainly before any regional comparison" as the example: this "worth [knowing/stating/naming/asking/raising] [directly/plainly/honestly]:" construction announces the act of stating something honestly instead of just stating it, "by saying it at all you are already doing what the AI part said it was going to do." A scan across every `lib/digest/*.ts` file found this far more pervasive than visible from any one entry: roughly 1,270+ occurrences across 47 of 59 content files, essentially the entire narrative content base.

Fixed via a careful, staged, scripted pass rather than one blind find-replace, specifically because many instances carry embedded content that matters (a live conditional like "if antithyroid drug treatment is already underway") between the announcement and the colon that a blind deletion would have destroyed, not just removed filler. Three verified-safe passes removed 581 instances across 41 files: sentence-initial "Worth [verb] [pure adverbs]: X" (capitalizing X to start the new sentence), the same construction mid-sentence following a noun phrase ("a practical consequence worth knowing directly: X" → "a practical consequence: X", keeping the colon the noun phrase structurally needs), and an expanded set of confirmed pure-meta "rather than [dishonest-framing-verb]" tails that describe the manner of presentation, not separate content. A first version of the mid-sentence pass had a bug (deleting the connecting colon along with the phrase, breaking several sentences) caught immediately via spot-checking the actual diffs before being committed anywhere, `lib/digest/` reverted to the last clean commit, and redone correctly; a handful of resulting ", :"/"and :" artifacts (where a leading comma or "and" no longer had anything to connect to once the announcement was removed) were found via a full-file grep sweep and hand-corrected individually. `tsc`/`eslint` clean across every touched file.

**Not implied complete:** roughly 650-700 occurrences remain, confirmed by the same scan. These split into two harder categories deliberately left for continued work rather than risked with a blind script: colon-anchored cases carrying a qualifying clause that changes the meaning ("if pregnancy is being planned after any past Graves' treatment," "since it lands differently for different thyroid conditions") and needs individual rewording to preserve that content while dropping only the announcement, and a no-colon trailing-clause form ("...a hidden additive worth knowing about, and a medication class that...") that wasn't targeted at all in this pass. A false-positive risk was also found and excluded: "worth" as an ordinary noun of value or quantity ("$X worth of Y per serving") matches the same surface pattern and must not be touched. This is the same "ongoing, multi-session" shape the Digest depth work and the Glossary expansion already follow, not a claim that the phrase no longer exists anywhere. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Second round, same day, direct request to keep going now.** Covered both harder categories named above: the no-colon trailing form (a new, carefully dry-run-tested pass, distinguishing "the pattern IS worth taking seriously" as its own predicate claim, left alone, from "an age-dependent healing timeline worth knowing honestly." as redundant commentary tacked onto an already-stated fact, dropped) and a chunk of the colon-anchored qualifier cases where the connector clause carries content that matters (restructured, not deleted: "worth knowing plainly for anyone encountering an older reference to the original 2013 paper: X" became "For anyone encountering an older reference to the original 2013 paper, X").

Three bugs in the earlier round's own work were found and fixed while dry-running this pass carefully before applying it, none had been confirmed on-device yet: (1) a punctuation artifact from the prior mid-sentence transform left a stray space before the colon in ~120 places ("a practical consequence : X" instead of "a practical consequence: X"), plus the analogous bug before periods and commas in ~50 more, all found via a full-file grep sweep (confirmed absent from every untouched file first, to rule out any pre-existing legitimate use) and fixed globally; (2) one of these accidentally touched code, not prose, a ternary operator in `index.ts` lost its own spacing, caught and reverted; (3) an early version of the no-colon pass would have deleted legitimate predicate usage ("concerns are actually worth watching" is its own claim, not decoration) because its own exclusion check only looked at the word immediately before "worth," missing "are actually worth" -- caught in a dry run before ever touching a file, not after.

**A scope clarification, not just more of the same pattern:** "worth discussing/raising/confirming with a doctor/cardiologist/nephrologist" (61 occurrences found) is a categorically different use of the word, actionable self-advocacy guidance (raise this with your own doctor), not the self-referential "announcing what's about to be stated" tic the original report named. Left untouched deliberately, not overlooked, this app's own Self Advocacy category and its whole "talk to your doctor about X" framing depends on exactly this kind of sentence. Three instances already touched before this distinction was drawn (gout.ts, graves.ts, lupus.ts, all "worth raising directly with a [professional]: X" turned into a direct imperative) were left as committed, a reasonable rewording either way, not reverted.

`tsc`/`eslint` clean across every touched file, artifact sweep re-run clean after every stage. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Third round, same day, continued "keep going now": the "worth stating plainly" sweep finished across the entire Digest content base.** Worked file by file through every remaining file with non-legitimate instances, largest first: gout, sjögrens, psoriasis, chronicKidneyDisease, type2Diabetes, migraine, multipleSclerosis, prostateHealth, celiac, type1Diabetes, foodIndustryHistory, rheumatoidArthritis, ibs, pcos, fattyLiverDisease, ibd, lifestyleEnvironment, lupus, recipes, popularDiets, glossary, homeGardening, neurogenesis, selfAdvocacy, foodAdditives, hormones, nutrients, otherAutoimmune, portionsAndRDAs, complementaryTherapies, organSystems, problemFoods, produceProfiles, and the remaining single-instance files (appHelps, fermentedFoods, gutMicrobiome, healingStages, history, labsMedication, mitochondriaMetabolism, preventionLifestyle, readingLabels, sleepHealth). Each fix restructured the sentence to keep the actual content (a qualifying clause, a cross-reference, a caveat) while dropping only the redundant announcement, same discipline as the first two rounds; a handful of pre-existing, unrelated grammar slips (a/an errors, stray commas, one broken sentence in graves.ts, one in pcos.ts) were fixed in passing since they sat inside text already being touched. Deliberately left alone throughout, confirmed legitimate rather than skipped: predicate usage ("the pattern IS worth taking seriously"), the self-advocacy "worth discussing/raising/asking ... with a doctor/specialist" construction (and its unquoted variants, "to a doctor," "at a next appointment," "with an [specialist]," all the same actionable pattern), the "worth reading/discussing alongside X" cross-reference form, and instances sitting inside `//` code comments (not customer-facing).

**A gap found and closed on top of that, not just more of the same sweep.** After believing the pass complete, a stray grep on `cardiovascularDisease.ts` (a file already marked done) turned up two live instances the classifier script had wrongly cleared: its own predicate-usage exclusion checked a 30-character lookback window for "is/are/was/were," which was wide enough to catch an unrelated "is" from earlier in the same sentence (in "disease is recognized and treated, worth knowing directly...," the "is" belongs to "disease is recognized," not to "worth") and wrongly treat the match as a legitimate claim. A stricter reclassification script (linking verb required immediately adjacent to "worth," not just present somewhere nearby) found 83 total instances across every file, all individually re-checked by hand; roughly 20 turned out to be the same false-negative pattern and were fixed (cardiovascularDisease.ts, sjögrens.ts, prostateHealth.ts, essentialNutrients.ts, graves.ts, chronicKidneyDisease.ts, recipes.ts, foodIndustryHistory.ts, gout.ts, pcos.ts, fattyLiverDisease.ts, fermentedFoods.ts, lifestyleEnvironment.ts, mentalHealth.ts, a file not touched in the first two rounds at all), the rest confirmed legitimate on manual review. `mentalHealth.ts` (the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline entry) is the one previously-unaudited file this closing pass caught. `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint lib/digest/*.ts` both clean project-wide after every file and again at the very end; a full punctuation-artifact sweep (stray space before a colon/period/comma, the same class of self-inflicted bug caught in round 2) came back clean except the one pre-existing, correct TypeScript ternary in `index.ts` already confirmed safe in round 2. One self-inflicted syntax break happened and was caught immediately by the routine post-edit `tsc` check: an edit to `portionsAndRDAs.ts` introduced an unescaped apostrophe inside a single-quoted string ("doesn't"), fixed the same turn it appeared. The construction can now be considered swept from the app: what remains anywhere in `lib/digest/` is confirmed, individually-reviewed legitimate content, not the redundant announcement pattern originally reported. 48 files touched, 386 lines changed. **Not yet confirmed on-device.**

**Also 2026-08-23: the actual Basic Health slowness root-caused and fixed, and the header-legibility saga's true final root cause found, after direct pushback that the shadow-only fix wasn't showing up even post-reinstall.** Basic Health's ~5-second display delay was never a caching problem (the earlier `useMemo` fix, while correct, wasn't the bottleneck): `BasicHealthShelves` was rendering all 479 Basic Health entries across roughly 21 groups eagerly via `ScrollView` + `.map()`, with zero virtualization, mounting hundreds of components before anything could paint. Converted each shelf's horizontal row to a `FlatList` with `getItemLayout` (fixed-width cards, `SHELF_CARD_WIDTH`/`SHELF_CARD_GAP`/`SHELF_CARD_STRIDE` constants replace the old hardcoded numbers), so only the visible cards in each row mount, and `scrollToIndex` replaces the old manual `onLayout`-tracked `ScrollView.scrollTo({x})`. Separately, re-investigating why the header fix "still doesn't work" after a full reinstall found a second bug the shadow-only fix never touched: `shelfCardSelected` (the state a shelf card enters the moment it's opened and read, the normal way anyone would hit "Essential Nutrients: Magnesium") was overriding `shelfCard`'s 85%-opaque `colors.surface` background with `${TAB_COLOR}22`, roughly 13% opaque, letting the photo blaze straight through behind the very text being read; fixed by dropping that override (the thicker accent border already marks selected state on its own). `shelfHeading` (the Basic Health group labels like "Essential Nutrients") also had no card or background behind it at all, not even a shadow's own contrast to sit against. All four title styles (`cardTitle`, `shelfCardTitle`, `shelfHeading`, plus `categoryHeaderText` from the prior pass) now carry a solid `rgba(0,0,0,0.55)` background chip directly on the text, not just a shadow, guaranteeing legibility regardless of what card or photo region sits behind them. `tsc`/`eslint` clean. **Not yet confirmed on-device** (Metro restarted with the fix live; awaiting a reload and check).

**Also 2026-08-23: header/label legibility fixed against real photo backgrounds, direct report.** Confirmed on-device: with the new Food and shared-field photo backgrounds actually showing (`GatedTabContent`'s always-correct gated-behind-`revealed` behavior, unrelated to this bug, just what finally exposed it), several headers had nothing behind them to stay readable against a bright patch of photo. Root cause, not a regression from anything done today: `PageIdentityLabel.tsx` (the "which lens am I in" box shown on every single tab) was deliberately built with a border but no fill, "so whatever's already behind it shows straight through," a real assumption from when that was always a calm background, now fixed with the same `rgba(0,0,0,0.55)` value already used everywhere else in this app for exactly this job (InfoAlert, PasswordPrompt, BusyOverlay, AppActionSheet). Digest's own `shelfHeading` (the "Diet & Food"-style group labels sitting above each horizontal shelf row) had no shadow or background at all, fixed with `menuLabelShadow`, the same shadow already tuned 2026-08-21 for TabHub/LensHub's own labels against a busy surface, not a new one invented here. **Direct follow-up correction, same day: that wasn't actually the problem being reported.** The real complaint was individual entry titles inside each Digest topic, "Essential Nutrients: Magnesium" named directly as an example, unreadable despite "the correct color." Real root cause, found by actually checking rather than re-guessing: `colors.surface` (the background every Digest card uses, `cardTitle`, `categoryHeaderText`, `shelfCardTitle`) is `rgba(..., 0.85)`, 85% opaque by design, not fully solid, reads as solid against this app's own dark ground theme but lets a bright patch of photo bleed through the remaining 15%, and none of these titles carried a shadow of their own to fall back on. The selected state of a shelf card is even more exposed, a `${TAB_COLOR}22` fill, roughly 13% opaque. Fixed by adding `menuLabelShadow` to all three (`cardTitle`, `categoryHeaderText`, `shelfCardTitle`), the earlier `PageIdentityLabel`/`shelfHeading` fixes both correct and left in place, just not what was actually being reported.

**Also fixed, same conversation, a real separate performance bug:** "why does it take so long for Basic Health to display?" `basicHealthAllGroups(entries)`, real, non-trivial work walking all ~21 Basic Health topics and filtering the full entry list once per topic, was called directly inline in this screen's own JSX, not memoized, rerunning on every render of the whole screen while Basic Health was open, not just once when first selected. `categorySearchGroups` a few lines above already got this right; the same `useMemo` pattern now applies to the plain browsing path too (`basicHealthGroups`). `tsc` clean project-wide, `eslint` clean on the touched file. **Not yet confirmed on-device, either fix.**

**Also 2026-08-23: "How Not to Die" (2025 documentary, Dean Ornish and Caldwell Esselstyn among its interviewed physicians) fact-checked against the peer-reviewed literature, direct request.** New `lib/digest/plantBasedNutrition.ts` (Basic Health): the Lifestyle Heart Trial (Ornish, Lancet 1990, PMID 1973470, a real RCT with hard angiographic outcomes, coronary stenosis regressed in the intervention group and progressed in the control group over one year, tiered `moderate` rather than `strong` specifically for its small size, 48 people total) and Esselstyn's own long-running case series (18 patients, disease arrest in every one, partial reversal in several, tiered `weak` on study design alone despite genuinely long follow-up, no control group). Real overlap check done first, not assumed: TMAO as a cardiovascular risk marker and the IARC processed-meat/colorectal-cancer classification were both already covered elsewhere in this Digest (`cardiovascularDisease.ts`, `foodAdditives.ts`) and are cross-linked, not duplicated. Two condition-specific applications added: `cardiovascularDisease.ts` gets the "already diagnosed, not just prevention" framing; `prostateHealth.ts` gets Ornish's separate 2005 prostate-cancer lifestyle trial (PMID 16094059, PSA and lab-dish markers, honestly flagged as surrogate endpoints, not confirmed progression or survival data), a genuinely new study type alongside that category's own already-substantial lycopene/cruciferous/choline-TMAO coverage, not a duplicate of it. **Second pass for full breadth, same day, direct request.** Four more real, independently-verified condition entries: Type 2 Diabetes (`type2-low-fat-vegan-diet-rct`, Barnard 2006, PMID 16873779, a real RCT reported honestly, its primary between-group comparison fell just short of significance, p=0.089, only a secondary analysis excluding medication-changers reached significance); Chronic Kidney Disease (`ckd-plant-based-diet-incidence-risk`, Dang 2025, PMID 40081608, a 121,927-person meta-analysis, OR 0.75 for developing CKD at all, checked directly against and confirmed genuinely distinct from that category's own pre-existing protein-source-management entry, incidence risk versus disease management); MASLD/Fatty Liver Disease (`masld-vegetarian-diet-rct-weight-loss-mechanism`, a 220-person Chinese RCT paired deliberately with a second, more recent trial that complicates the headline finding, weight loss and reduced ultra-processed food intake, not the vegetarian label itself, predicted the improvement, included on purpose rather than left out for being less flattering); and Gout (`gout-whole-food-plant-based-pilot-rct`, a small 33-person pilot RCT, real, statistically significant uric-acid and pain reduction, honestly flagged as needing a larger confirmatory trial). The remaining conditions (the full autoimmune group, Migraine, IBS, Celiac, PCOS, Type 1 Diabetes) were checked and correctly left without an entry: this documentary's own claims run through cardiometabolic mechanisms, not the autoimmune-trigger or single-nutrient mechanisms those conditions' research is actually built on, and no direct, citable connection turned up for any of them. `tsc` clean project-wide, `eslint` clean on every touched/created file.

**Also 2026-08-21, the header/footer line saga, resolved: it was never the footer line at all.** After the `footerLine` bug (`ScreenBackground.tsx`, Home's own separate copy, `ScreenHeader.tsx`'s divider) was found and removed outright, the same faint line kept showing on every screen anyway, footer band and Profile alike, surviving a fully cache-cleared Metro restart and a hard app restart. The actual source: `components/AppKeyboard.tsx`. It's the one component in this app mounted globally, once, on top of every screen (`app/_layout.tsx`), and its own `container` style has a `borderTopWidth: 1`. It happened to sit at almost the exact same position `footerLine` did, which is why fixing that bug first didn't fix the symptom; it just stopped masking a second, unrelated issue underneath it. Confirmed via a clean diagnostic (temporarily disabling `AppKeyboard` entirely): "The line is finally gone." The hide animation's translateY math and its `activeField`/`progress` state both check out correctly on paper, so this reads as `overflow: 'hidden'` not reliably clipping a Reanimated-transformed child at the Android compositor level, not a logic error in the file. Fixed by animating `opacity` to 0 alongside the existing `translateY`, an independent mechanism from the transform-based clip. `tsc`/`eslint` clean, confirmed live in a forced bundle. Root cause confirmed on-device via the diagnostic; the fix itself (keyboard re-enabled, opacity added) is **not yet separately confirmed on-device.**
